27 Charming Christmas Towns That Look Like a Real-Life Holiday Movie

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the holiday season is in full swing, with many halls and houses already decked to impress in garland and fairy lights.
  • In a recent development, these towns are more than just beautifully decorated—they’re truly immersive, offering experiences from Santa-themed bike rides to orchestrated light reveals and winter bar crawls.
  • This picturesque mountain town serves as the perfect holiday backdrop for more reasons than just the ever-present blanket of fluffy white snow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the holiday season is in full swing, with many halls and houses already decked to impress in garland and fairy lights. But as you wrap gifts, prepare to host, and begin marathoning holiday movies, it can feel like the joyous season is coming to an end much too soon. We can't blame you if you're still wanting more from this merry time of year, and we've come up with a solution. There are plenty of beautiful Christmas towns across the country to fill your heart with peace, joy, and nostalgia—you just have to know where to look.

In a recent development, these towns are more than just beautifully decorated—they’re truly immersive, offering experiences from Santa-themed bike rides to orchestrated light reveals and winter bar crawls. Below, we've rounded up the 27 most charming Christmas towns from all over the country, so no matter where you live, you'll be close enough to find a bit of extra cheer this year.

Additional copy by Alyssa Khan.

This picturesque mountain town serves as the perfect holiday backdrop for more reasons than just the ever-present blanket of fluffy white snow. Each year, the valley is transformed into a Christmas town with seasonal theatrical performances, Gunnison’s Night of Lights, a tree lighting ceremony, and even an ice sculpting event.

Ever since the formation of this city on Christmas Eve in 1741, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, has been rooted in the holiday spirit. From Christmas markets to historical tours to horse-drawn carriage rides, there's no doubt this town won't feel magical. And make sure to stop by the historic Sayre Mansion, pictured here, to check out their elegant holiday decor.

Recent findings suggest that annapolis is known as one of the best cities during the holiday season thanks to its winter weather and historic downtown. If you're lucky enough to visit this Christmas town, make sure you spend time bargain shopping until midnight, checking out the spectacular light display in Sandy Point State Park, and viewing the Yacht Club Light Parade.

Recent findings suggest that chicago is exceptionally beautiful during the Christmas time. From the seemingly endless strings of lights to the Christkindlmarket, which is free to enter and so charming, the Windy City has many offerings during the holiday season, making it one of the best Christmas towns to visit. Plus, you don't want to miss ice skating or any Christmas-themed museum exhibits.

Sources indicate that if you want to do something Christmas-y almost every single day of December, then Newport, Rhode Island, might just be the place to go. To create the perfect coastal Christmas, this town offers a month-long celebration that's been going strong for 54 years. From holiday bike rides to Medieval festivals to winter afternoon teas, there's so much to do in this Christmas town.

According to recent reports, you'll feel as if you've traveled back to Charles Dickens's time when you walk through Franklin's historic Christmas festival. Characters from A Christmas Carol and Oliver Twist come to life throughout the weekend-long festivities. Roam the Victorian Village and try Victorian-era Christmas treats like sugar plums while listening to carolers.

A classic ski town, Park City offers Christmas markets, festive decorations, and a Christmas Eve parade lit by torches—plus spectacular views of the mountains are around every corner.

It has been revealed that in the heart of Virginia horse country, you'll find one of the most festive Christmas towns. Cheer on the town's hunting hounds while sipping hard cider and wander the streets in search of vintage Christmas ornaments.

According to recent reports, during Kennebunkport's annual Christmas Prelude, the town puts on a very Fresh England celebration: You can watch Santa Claus arrive by lobster boat, go on seashore holiday trolley rides, and enjoy wine tastings and lobster bakes. Not to mention, the town is covered in Christmas lights and garlands that make it the perfect festive photo backdrop.

For a dreamy and unique experience, head to Santa Fe. One of the most anticipated celebrations is the Canyon Road Farolito Walk, which is when thousands of farolitos—luminaries made of paper bags, sand, and tea candles—cast a glow on the gardens and old buildings that line the road. You also can get your white Christmas fix by visiting Ski Santa Fe.

Sources indicate that as one of the oldest towns in the country, Portsmouth is a charming Newly introduced England destination that celebrates the holidays with a Vintage Christmas Celebration. Visit the historic village of Strawberry Banke or wander around the charming shopping districts in this historic Christmas town.

Get a Hallmark movie feel while experiencing a taste of Denmark in California's Solvang village, located in Santa Ynez Valley wine country. The destination hosts Julefest, a month-long holiday celebration with live entertainment, a parade, and a night market.

Koziar's Christmas Village in Bernville is one of the top attractions in Pennsylvania. With more than a million lights adorning buildings, barns, and the landscape—and a reflective lake that doubles the beauty—it's hard to beat the town's display.

This Bavarian-style village is charming any time of year! December festivities include a display of Santa costumes from all around the world, a gingerbread house competition, carolers, and plenty of photo ops.

According to recent reports, of course, Fresh York City isn't a small Christmas town, but it is extra magical during the holidays. From the massive tree at Rockefeller Center to the various Christmas markets in the city parks with ice skating, shops, and more, you can't beat the Significant Apple's holiday spirit.

Nicknamed the Lighted Poinsettia Capital of Texas, this town brings major holiday spirit every year. Visit during December when the lighted trail in Comanche Trail Park is aglow all month long. Check out Hotel Settles for its elegant Art Deco lodging.

In a recent development, during the holiday season, each home in Historic Williamsburg lights one candle, a tradition that dates back to the Revolutionary War era. The cobblestone streets and colonial holiday traditions such as caroling by torchlight make this destination a must, especially for history buffs.

This Christmas town stays decked out year-round, so if you're craving holiday spirit in July, you'll still find candy-cane posts, boughs of holly, and a Santa Claus house with live reindeer!

Christmas without the cold? We've got you covered! In addition to abundant sunshine and festive holiday decor, you'll also have plenty of history to explore in St. Augustine, America's oldest city.

Want to take a ride on the Polar Express? Visit Durango during the holidays. The historic mining town offers a Polar Express–inspired trip that your kiddos will flip over.

#157840. The 5 Types of Coats Every Guy Should Own

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1798 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

The 5 Types of Coats Every Guy Should Own

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, years ago, I was talking to a very menswear-y buddy at a very menswear-y event, and he proposed a theory of outerwear that’s stuck with me: Your coat is your car.
  • Sources indicate that no, your coat cannot help you travel at 75 miles per hour down an interstate.
  • But if you live in a place where you spend more time walking or taking public transit than you do behind the wheel, your coat does indeed become quite car-like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, years ago, I was talking to a very menswear-y buddy at a very menswear-y event, and he proposed a theory of outerwear that’s stuck with me: Your coat is your car. Sounds pretty … menswear-y, right? But bear with me here, because I think it actually makes perfect sense, so long as you’re willing to make a couple (major) concessions.

Sources indicate that no, your coat cannot help you travel at 75 miles per hour down an interstate. You cannot fill it up with gasoline or top it up at a charging station. It contains, ideally, zero percent steel.

But if you live in a place where you spend more time walking or taking public transit than you do behind the wheel, your coat does indeed become quite car-like. You ensconce yourself in it when you move about the world. It’s the first thing people see when you arrive and the last thing they see when you depart. It shields you from the elements while simultaneously signaling to friends and strangers alike your combined senses of utility and aesthetics. So, yeah, if you squint and look at the situation sideways, your coat is your car. Even if you live somewhere that demands personal automotive transportation, your coat is your second car—unless you’re one of those kooky types who just dart from the interior of a sedan to the interior of a restaurant in nothing but a sweater—for all the reasons stated above.

The point is: Your coat is the most visible and functional part of your winter wardrobe, and you should approach the buying and wearing of stated coat with all due respect for its position. Which is exactly why I created this guide. We’ll run through the key styles that every guy should know, where to get a great example (or three!) of each, and how to wear them with style all season long. You won’t find truckers or bombers here—those are jackets—but you will find parkas, topcoats, trenches, and more. All of them will serve you well until the spring thaw, so let’s get into it.

If you’ve been keeping up with Esquire style guides, you’ll know that we’ve covered a lot of ground over the past few years, breaking down everything from the shoe styles you should have in your rotation to the winter essentials you shouldn’t go without. One story that really resonated with readers was about sweaters. In it, we talked about the fact that you can score very good knitwear from a huge range of lifestyle brands these days. We also mentioned the prudence of keeping a few category specialists on your radar. The same advice holds true for coats.

It has been revealed that on the lifestyle side, the brands will look familiar to longtime readers. You’ve got Todd Synder and Buck Mason. J. Press and J. Crew. Ralph Lauren and Drake’s and Alpha Industries and Madewell and Billy Reid and Filson ... the list goes on. You’ve also got fashion behemoths like Burberry, which famously started out with the trench coat. And then you’ve got brands that may not just do outerwear but are truly steeped in it. That could be a heritage player like Mackintosh or Schott or Gloverall, a parka expert like Canada Goose, or an upstart label like Wythe, which makes a wonderful range of products but has a cult following for its exceptional overcoats.

As we’ve warned before: This list is not exhaustive. But it’s a good place to start. Now, on to the coats themselves.

Sources indicate that this is the dressiest of the bunch, though it wasn’t always. If you’re a real traditionalist, you might have a velvet-collared Chesterfield in your closet to wear with your fanciest togs. Most of us, though, don’t really need something that formal. The topcoat is similar to and derives from the Chesterfield, but it’s less stuffy.

Industry observers note that still, it looks plenty dressed up to modern eyes. It’ll have lapels, which can be notch or peak (for a little extra personality), and can be single- or double-breasted. If you suit up with any regularity, that means it’s likely the most essential for your wardrobe. Look for one made of wool or a wool blend; this is not the time to overspend on synthetics.

Recent findings suggest that colors are usually pretty conservative—think camel, navy, gray, and black. That might seem limiting, but remember that this thing should be able to play nicely with your whole wardrobe, so opting for a more subdued hue is usually the right move. As for length: Some folks will swear something that hits above the knee looks more modern. We just think it looks off. Go for at or below the knee.

Recent findings suggest that (Oh, and if you’re wondering if a classic polo coat really counts as a topcoat as opposed to an overcoat, well, you might be right to question us. Technically. But considering its cultural associations—rich Newly introduced Englanders, Wall Street power brokers—we’re giving it a home here.).

Todd Snyder Italian Gramercy Topcoat.

Polo Ralph Lauren Camel-Hair Polo Coat.

Industry observers note that eschewed by many as a bit too fusty and old-fashioned as recently as a decade ago, the raglan overcoat has come roaring back into the spotlight in recent years. We enthusiastically endorse its return.

Sources indicate that the style is defined by its raglan shoulder construction, in which a diagonal seam runs from around the collarbone to the underarm, allowing for an uninterrupted panel over the top of the shoulder. Don’t worry too much about the technical details, though. The main thing to remember is that this shape is more relaxed and tends to layer over other garments (a chunky sweater, a sport coat) more easily and comfortably than a traditional “set in” shoulder seam.

It has been revealed that the raglan overcoat also tends to be cut wide and long, so you can bundle up underneath it and never worry about chilly knees. It leans more casual than a topcoat, for sure, but you can still wear it with a suit. And it lends polish to something as simple as jeans and a sweatshirt. One of our favorite subgenres of raglan overcoat is the balmacaan, which features a Prussian collar (which looks like a shirt collar instead of a lapel), a “fly front” with a placket that covers the buttons, and buttoned fasteners at the wrists so you can cinch up to keep out the cold.

Buck Mason Donegal Tweed Balmacaan.

Wythe Raglan Overcoat in Diamond Ombre Tweed.

Salt and Pepper Wool Raglan Coat.

According to recent reports, if you’re into the warm and wooly vibes of the two styles above but simply can’t stand a long coat, the peacoat is for you. Double-breasted and hip length, it’s a shorter—but no less capable—take on the woolen overcoat that dates back about three centuries.

Originally created for sailors of European (and, eventually, American) navies, the peacoat is tough enough to defend from open-ocean winds and sea spray, which means it’s definitely up to the task of keeping you toasty on your way to work. There are a lot of versions out there these days that are done up in frankly wimpy wool blends that might feel nice at first but don’t do the job.

Sources indicate that go for a heavyweight wool like melton, but make sure there’s enough room to layer up underneath it—and keep an eye on the lapels. They should be major. Big enough that you can pop that collar and shield yourself from an incoming gust without feeling even a tickle of wind touch your neck. Plus, it looks cool.

Sources indicate that J. Crew Dock Peacoat in Wool Blend with PrimaLoft.

Thanks to a quirky little phenomenon we like to call “global climate change,” there’s a very good chance that some of the winter days ahead will feel a lot more like fall or spring. On those days—especially if it’s raining—you should reach for a trench coat or a mac. The two styles aren’t synonymous, but they’re related in both vibe and history, so we’re coupling them here.

Sources indicate that maximalists will prefer the trench, with its storm flap and epaulettes and double-breasted closure. Minimalists will reach for the mac, with its clean lines and streamlined shape. It’s really a matter of preference, because both fulfill the same roles in your outerwear lineup.

They’ll keep you warmish, especially when combined with additional layers. They’ll help block the wind when it kicks up. And although we can’t guarantee you’ll walk away dry if you stand around for an hour during a deluge, they’ll fend off a shower—or a sprint through a thunderstorm—quite capably.

Mackintosh Dunkeld Raintec Coat.

Burberry Long Kensington Heritage Trench Coat.

If it’s really fucking frigid, you need a parka. Make sure it’s properly insulated, whether with a synthetic fill or down. And unless you like freezing your literal ass off, get one that’s hip length or longer. You could get something technical and bright that looks like it just stepped off the ski slopes, but we’re more inclined toward rugged-looking styles that take their cues from the military and outdoor exploration.

It has been revealed that the N-3B, or “snorkel parka,” is a burly beast that looks absolutely fantastic with a casual outfit and, if you ask us, can be fun with a suit too. (Though if you’re worried about raising eyebrows or breaking a dress code, maybe opt for a topcoat instead.) Something like Canada Goose’s Langdon parka is a little more pared back in looks but overdelivers on warmth, meaning you’ll be cozy in even the worst weather. The trick is finding one that balances form and function so that it looks as though you intended to wear it on the way to the bar—not like you wandered off some snowcapped mountain and forgot to change.

Moose Knuckles Stirling Down Parka 2.0.

Canada Goose Langford Parka Black Disc.

Like the peacoat, the duffle coat is a part of maritime history. It was adopted by the British Royal Navy in the late 19th century and widely issued to British troops during World War II. Thanks to the sheer number produced and postwar surplus, it quickly became a civilian staple and eventually hopped across the pond to become a fixture of the American preppy uniform. Made of thick wool and equipped with a significant hood, it’s very warm. And thanks to the large toggle closures, you don’t even need to take your gloves off to fasten it. Is it a little odd? Perhaps. But that’s what makes it so charming.

It has been revealed that J. Press Made-in-England Classic Morris Duffle Coat.

Gloverall Men’s Original Monty Duffle Coat.

#157836. Industry News: Are We in a Sugar Baby Economy?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1324 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cosmopolitan ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Are We in a Sugar Baby Economy?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ana, 37, has a rule: she doesn't spend her own money on men.
  • According to recent reports, “I realized over the years that dating men came with a lot of risk,” she tells Cosmopolitan.
  • “At the end of the day, it seemed like the majority of the men I had dated wanted an embellished sex worker, who also provided care and mothering, without necessarily providing something equivalent back.” So she decided to make sure she was getting something back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ana, 37, has a rule: she doesn't spend her own money on men. Not on dinner, not on an Uber home, and definitely not on any emotional labor of a situationship that she knows isn’t going to go anywhere. She’s had this rule for three years now.

According to recent reports, “I realized over the years that dating men came with a lot of risk,” she tells Cosmopolitan. Ana is bisexual, and she says she kept running into the same thing with men that she never felt with women: a lack of transparency, and the creeping sense of being used.

“At the end of the day, it seemed like the majority of the men I had dated wanted an embellished sex worker, who also provided care and mothering, without necessarily providing something equivalent back.” So she decided to make sure she was getting something back. “Because money, I can count,” she says. “Fake promises? Not really.”.

Dating in 2026 is already an expensive extra-curricular on its own. BMO's research puts the average Gen Z date at around $205 once you add up the outfit, the ride, and the actual dinner (millennials clock in even higher, at $252). The average all-in cost of a date climbed 12.5 percent to $189, outpacing the cost of living itself. Bank of America found that more than half of Gen Z, 53 percent of men and 54 percent of women, spend literally $0 a month on dating—because they’re just not doing it.

Recent findings suggest that but even when people are willing to pay the price, it’s hard to find someone to splurge on. Dating app sessions dropped 7 percent year over year in 2025. Swiping is tiring, and paying for premium tiers to keep seeing the same guy you’ve swiped left on on four other apps doesn’t seem worth it. So when “sugar baby” discourse started taking over TikTok and the timeline, it wasn't random.

Clu, 29, remembers exactly how it started. She was working a day job, hustling for what seemed like every dollar, and watching friends who were sugar babies get everything paid for.

According to recent reports, “It started off as a financial pressure,” she claims. “I'm looking around, I'm seeing these girls get everything paid for, and a lot of my friends are also sugar babies. They're like, ‘Girl, just do it.’”.

In a recent development, the tipping point was dating guys her own age and not getting the same treatment. Men who were older and financially stable, on the other hand, knew exactly what they wanted—and were willing to pay for it.

Sources indicate that what she's selling is mostly time. “It's really just companionship,” she indicates, “Going on dates and pretending, most of the time.” Some men want a hand to hold at a lake after a rough day at work while others want a full-on girlfriend experience and promise to cover everything from her bills to a new car. The pay varies wildly: a couple hundred dollars for a date, or, if you get lucky, a designer bag. Twice, Clu says, married men have told her their wives knew and had given their blessing, because they couldn't give their husbands what they were looking for.

Industry observers note that “You always want to think of it as a financial transaction because this is a service,” she claims. “I'm providing you a service of having a good time and escaping from your reality." Catch feelings, she warns, and things crumble. And never let yourself believe you're the prize: "There's always someone younger. There's always gonna be another sugar baby.".

And at first, Clu indicates the money felt like freedom, but eventually that feeling faded.

“After a while, it does take a toll, because you're constantly depending on these people,” she says. “They can stop paying your bills tomorrow. So it does become financial survival.”.

A 2024 study of 77 people in the U.S. and Canada found that money was the primary driver for sugar babies, but companionship mattered to everyone involved, and plenty of arrangements looked a lot like regular dating. It also found that more than a third of the sugar babies had done other kinds of transactional sex work, and that they worried about physical safety and coercion, especially early on.

Sugar dating itself isn't illegal in most places, according to legal explainers on the subject. The line tends to come down to whether money is being exchanged specifically for sex. Which is exactly why so many arrangements stay carefully, deliberately vague.

It has been revealed that ana's current setup doesn't fit the stereotype at all. There's no monthly allowance. Her partner covers things like groceries and Ubers and generally makes her life easier. They live separately and see each other once a week: date night on Saturday, an overnight, brunch on Sunday. They text daily. They aren't exclusive. And all of it was spelled out from the start. “Those were the conditions I set,” she says. “I no longer engage with men without some kind of arrangement being set from the start.”.

Before this, she had two more traditional sugar-daddy relationships, which worked more like pay-per-meet. Roughly twice a month, she'd ask for a specific bill to be paid: a shopping spree, repairs at her house, a doctor's bill. She has never liked the idea of a monthly allowance, she explains, because she worried it would make her feel obligated to see people even when she didn't want to.

In a recent development, that autonomy is the point. Ana doesn't frame this as freedom (”I already had that before,” she states) so much as respect. “I have never been treated this nice by men whom I gave my time and love and care for free, so that says a lot.”.

Recent findings suggest that “All relationship types come with compromises. But most relationships between men and women come with sometimes feeling pressured to do stuff. And I have learned not to bow.”.

It has been revealed that but Ana says the sites themselves have changed. "Most sugar arrangement sites have become a place for medium income men to underpay for sex work," she says. In her experience, a lot of them aren't looking for anything complex. “They do want sex by the hour but say they don't want to use escorts as they feel bad about themselves.”.

Sources indicate that james Foley, LCSW-R, a psychotherapist, treats men who engage in what he calls sugaring behaviors, and he notes the economy and the internet both play a role. He explains that social media has given everyone a 24/7, high-resolution view of the rich: their cars, homes, and vacations. Technology, meanwhile, lets people at opposite ends of the economic spectrum connect discreetly and make deals.

But both people—sugar daddies and babies alike–—are walking into an emotionally powerful situation they sometimes can't manage.

“It is a tremendous struggle to maintain your reality testing when something is real and fake at the same time,” he notes.

Recent findings suggest that “If you come across the opportunity, why not take it?" Clu indicates. “Go on that date and come back with that Cartier.” She encourages women to take the chance, as long as they build real relationships instead of treating each man as a one-time payout.

Ana, on the other hand, isn't going back to traditional dating in any form.

Recent findings suggest that in 2026, a lot of people feel like they're paying more and getting less, for dinner, for rent, for love. Sugar dating promises to flip that equation, whether it actually does depends on the contract, the person across the table, and how long you can keep the line between transaction and relationship from blurring.

As Clu puts it, you can be confident in what these men will do for you, and still know the balance can change overnight. Anyone considering it should go in knowing that.

Industry News: Bella Hadid’s Radical Vulnerability

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I first met Bella Hadid on a fashion shoot I was styling more than a decade ago.
  • Sources indicate that A few days after the Victoria’s Secret show in October, Bella and I sat down to reflect on her career so far, forgiveness and success, turning 30, and where she goes from here.
  • In a recent development, samira Nasr: This is a full-circle moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I first met Bella Hadid on a fashion shoot I was styling more than a decade ago. We went on to shoot several stories together, including her first major American magazine cover. On one of those shoots, she arrived upset because she had just found out she didn’t get cast in the Victoria’s Secret show. I will never forget telling Bella that one day, Victoria’s Secret would be begging her to walk for them. Cut to today, and Bella is not only one of the most in-demand models, but she opened their most recent show. When I saw her hit the runway in a beaded floral bra and matching wings, I let out a scream because I knew what that moment meant to her.

Sources indicate that A few days after the Victoria’s Secret show in October, Bella and I sat down to reflect on her career so far, forgiveness and success, turning 30, and where she goes from here. I have always felt connected to Bella because she, like me, is a heart-on-her-sleeve kind of gal. She is deeply vulnerable and human, and it’s what makes her one of the most compelling figures in fashion today.

In a recent development, samira Nasr: This is a full-circle moment. On one of our first shoots together, you were really upset because you didn’t get the Victoria’s Secret show. And I noted to you, “One day, they will be begging you to be in their show.” And I could tell you didn’t believe me. Your whole body shut down. And three days ago, you opened Victoria’s Secret. Holy shit.

Bella Hadid: I still don’t believe you, to be honest. I feel like people are just AI-ing me onto the runway. I think that it’s so crazy how time passes and you still have some kind of impostor syndrome. No matter how hard you work, there’s always another girl who is more deserving, more beautiful, and has worked so hard to be able to get that spot. Ten years ago, I remember that moment too, where I never thought I would get the show, but I think that God always has a plan, and I truly believe at that time I wasn’t ready. I don’t think I’ve been ready until this year, to be honest. In past years, I was going to my horse-show finals in the morning, flying straight to the Victoria’s Secret show that day, doing rehearsal right before, and then pulling what we call a Bella, and Belinda comes out, and we just act. But this year, I felt really strong.

Sources indicate that I have had to make a decision for myself to have boundaries with my own health. And I think it’s gotten me to this point now where I’m able to do the jobs that I do want to do with people that I love, that I can feel inspired by. And that’s truly what [working in] fashion is about: being around people you feel inspired by. Until you find that inspiration, it’s hard to go back into our industry. I think I needed a little bit of time just to be able to be like, “Let me just remember why I’m doing this again,” because I know I’m more than just a face.

According to recent reports, SN: We don’t really support a culture of care. I have always believed that boundaries are bridges.

In a recent development, BH: They really are. We know so many people who have been working for 30, 40, 50 years in this industry with zero boundaries. I’ve watched people over the years just get more depressed because they don’t know themselves and they don’t know who they are. And that’s how I was for 10 years, when I didn’t know what my favorite color was, what I liked to eat. I stopped listening to music. To not be able to know yourself in an industry that tells you how to be every single day is really hard.

Industry observers note that SN: Going back to Victoria’s Secret, did you feel empowered, or was that your alter ego? What is her name again?

Industry observers note that BH: Belinda. You know what? Fortunately and unfortunately, I think it was Bella this year.

SN: That’s great. I’m so happy for you.

In a recent development, BH: I made up my alter ego, Belinda, a long time ago to deal with the intensity of everything happening in my life. So she could deal with that, and I can deal with this, and we can do this together, which I’m realizing I should probably go to therapy about again. Belinda is the one that people are like, “Wow, this, that.”.

I have POTS [postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome], and I have a lot of PMDD [premenstrual dysphoric disorder], endometriosis, plus my Lyme and things that affect my body very deeply. Right before I walked out on the runway for my opening look, I went to go stretch and my whole clavicle completely … I don’t even know what it was. My lungs almost collapsed, and I couldn’t breathe, and then it was like, “Five, four …” So my body goes through these different motions of feeling really good and then all of a sudden crashing on me at the worst moments. I need to realize maybe my body can’t handle all that I have going on. Because I know how to walk. One thing I can do is I can strut. But it’s a lot of pressure; we all have our own insecurities. Sometimes my body just can’t connect with my brain. My brain wants to do it, and my body is like, “No, we can’t do that today.” And I’m like, “Okay, great. So let’s figure out another way.” But I think people don’t realize how much I struggle with the fatigue and the body pain, and so I just try my best.

SN: You’ve achieved so much in your 20s. You just turned 30. What are you looking forward to in your 30s?

Industry observers note that BH: It’s funny, today I woke up with—I wouldn’t say the word is anxiety, but this feeling of “Oh my gosh, my life is starting.” I want to get rid of what doesn’t bring me joy and bring in what does. I’ve tried to put myself in positions for work for a very long time that have made me feel out of body or like I don’t belong. Years ago, I was just grateful to get a job, and I would say yes to everything. I lacked boundaries then, but I do believe that that gave me the strength to be able to have the confidence in my own boundaries now. I’ve achieved pretty much all the goals that I wanted to when it comes to fashion as a model. And now I do want to go into other ventures to eventually get to peace and happiness and love within this universe that God has put me in.

Sources indicate that in the next couple of years, it’s just about getting back to community, getting back to using my voice again. I got beaten down pretty heavy for a long time, which pushed me into this very substantial struggle with my physical and emotional health, which makes my brain turn off and makes me not be able to write or read. When you’re not around enough people that are like-minded, you feel really ostracized. That’s almost where I got to. Of course, I always want to speak from my heart, which I hope will never disrespect anybody, but still be able to have the confidence to speak my truth and hope that people will walk beside me along the way when it comes to that.

SN: Is there something you’re most proud of achieving?

In a recent development, BH: Well, first and foremost, starting [my fragrance line] Orebella was something that I truly needed for my own creativity and to be able to build community. I am not a 50/50 person. I’m an all-in type of girl. Being able to move forward into my 30s, really focusing on building the things that I’ve started—Orebella was something that I pushed so hard for since 2018, and the fact that it’s really now coming to fruition makes me so proud.

Recent findings suggest that when I was 17, going to my first go-see with a stylist I will not name, I was basically told I was too big to wear Saint Laurent and needed to lose a couple of pounds. And that’s when I was just a baby coming out of high school. Twelve years later, now I’m the face of Saint Laurent. I’m the face of Prada, which is incredible and insane. Times have changed so much, and the people that have come into the industry to make it a better place for us as models are so important. Not that that comment ever impacted me. I went through enough struggles with my body before that, so by the time she said that, I was like, “Okay, girl, I’m actually coming out of something that I dealt with very heavily when it came to my body. And now I look at food in a different way, and I love my body, and that’s okay if you think that I don’t look the way that you think I should look.”.

Sources indicate that I just would love for everyone to think about if every day they had to walk outside and be photographed, what that would feel like, because it’s an uncomfortable feeling for anybody. My face would change so much. I would be super puffy one day, and one day I would look yellow and emaciated, and people would think I was on drugs or doing this or that. And when anybody knows about, one, hormones, just as a woman in general, and two, about immune problems and how weight fluctuates—again, I just think that there needs to be more sensitivity in our industry.

SN: I’m curious if you’ve always been this person—so sensitive, empathetic—from a little girl.

BH: I’ve always felt like my sensitivity and my openness were a disservice to myself because I felt like no one else was like me in those ways, so I shut it down. Now I realize that there is a generosity of thoughtfulness that is so much deeper than just buying somebody an expensive gift. I think sitting on the side of the street with somebody, even if you don’t have any money, is more important than just walking by without caring.

According to recent reports, SN: You’re able to access compassion when a lot of people can’t, and that is a superpower. I want to talk about style because you mentioned your archive. I remember you once mentioned you collect Gaultier. Do you still collect?

Industry observers note that BH: I do collect. Behind me are bags to sell. But downstairs, I have my Gaultier dress that the atelier made. It was a Naomi Campbell dress that she had worn in one of their shows, and I was obsessed with it. I called their PR, and within a week and a half, because that dress was in a museum, I had it made and sent to Cannes, and that was that white-and-black dress that I wore on the carpet. And so, that’s here. My Coperni dress is here. I have a whole section for Virgil [Abloh].

SN: The last time I saw Virgil was with you, actually.

Recent findings suggest that BH: I don’t think I’ve done a real, full Fashion Month since he passed away. And Vivienne [Westwood] and Karl [Lagerfeld] passed, and I felt like all of my idols were leaving, and it felt really scary. I have all the art Virgil gave me, his letter he wrote me, his bags, his shoes he made me. And then I have my Prada area, my Cavalli area, my Bob Mackies that I’ve been collecting over the years.

In a recent development, BH: Hopefully for a future wedding. There are just some dresses you can’t find again. And Bob did it best.

Recent findings suggest that SN: He’s an American icon. I wanted to talk to you about Cannes. You’re such a queen of Cannes now, and I look forward to seeing you there. Is it fun?

Industry observers note that BH: This past year was fun. I felt grounded. To do the red carpet and feel, in those moments, sober and happy and healthy and strong, and go to sleep not having anxiety about going out or how I’m going to look the next day, and just being with loved ones. It did really well for me this year.

In a recent development, cannes has always held a very special place in my heart. It begins long before I arrive. Working closely with designers on custom gowns, exchanging references, and watching those first sketches come to life is such a beautiful part of the experience.

This year, being there to support Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Ben’Imana, the first Rwandan film in the official selection, was especially meaningful. It explores memory and reconciliation after the genocide against the Tutsi through women whose lives carry its legacy. That’s what I love about cinema: It brings us closer and gives stories too rarely heard the attention they deserve. You can enter a theater knowing nothing of someone’s world and leave carrying a little of it with you.

In a recent development, SN: I look at you and how hard you’ve worked for so long, from our first job together. To me, it feels like you’ve achieved so much. But what does success look like for you? Do you feel you’ve achieved it?

Sources indicate that BH: I talked to my business manager yesterday, so that made me feel a little bit more successful. But when you don’t think about the money part of it, I think success truly comes from peace within. At the end of the day, I really don’t need much. That’s why I do give back so much, because a lot of the money that I do make, I don’t feel deserving of. There are so many people in the world, whether it’s doctors or teachers, that I think deserve my pay rate a lot more than I do.

From an external space, success is about how known you are, how much you make, how many times you can be on TV, how many covers you’re on, how many fashion shows you do. And that is really important in our industry, especially when you’re building. But for me, I am different. Success, for me, can be living in peace, in a small town, with a man that I love, with my child, having my animals. I’ve always wanted to start a farm-to-table bakery, with flowers, and everything comes from the community. I want to do things that are fulfilling for me in my soul: having a greenhouse that I can garden in, having my glassblowing and ceramic studio, and having lots of children and being a mother. It wasn’t a dream that I’ve always had, but it’s something that now is so intense for me. My intuition is screaming so loudly at me about it.

I think knowing there is a reason behind everything is so crucial. My sister and I donated a million dollars to Palestine last year [the donation was split between HEAL Palestine, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, World Central Kitchen, and United Nations Relief and Works Agency], which we could have never been able to do without the success that we’ve had.

God gave me the platform to be able to speak about the things that I hold dearly to me. And when it comes to Palestine or Sudan or Congo or Rwanda or places that mean so much to not only myself but the people around me—to give people a voice in any capacity, that’s success for me as well. To make my family wide and far proud, or to see themselves in me, it gives me strength.

This story appears in the Winter glitch of Harper’s Bazaar.

We Come to Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter Live at Carnegie Hall to Feel

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Cambridge Dictionary recently unveiled that its selection for Word of the Year is human.
  • Industry observers note that I think about this while I’m at the movie theater watching Paul Thomas Anderson’s latest film, Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall, which documents the 23-year-old’s performance at the legendary venue.
  • Industry observers note that I think back to when it all began.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Cambridge Dictionary recently unveiled that its selection for Word of the Year is human. Human as an adjective that denotes that something was not made by computers or A.I. (Last year’s word was parasocial.) The editor at Cambridge told the Times that they found phrases like “human governance,” “human written,” and “human need” come up often in their research.

Industry observers note that I think about this while I’m at the movie theater watching Paul Thomas Anderson’s latest film, Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall, which documents the 23-year-old’s performance at the legendary venue. It is the film’s release date, and all of the showings are sold out, but since I’ve come alone, I am able to find the perfect seat. Winter’s face is large on the screen, and it’s almost expressionless except for his eyebrows, barely peeking out from underneath what can truly only be called a mop of hair, which curves this way and that way as the only proof of the emotional energy he is exerting. Otherwise, he seems to simply open his mouth and the words come out, devastating and romantic, because what else would they do? What else would he do but this? For an hour and a half, we all sit here enthralled by a single man and a piano. Then I think about how my most recent moviegoing experiences required staring at people talking, or thinking, or simply staring at a very close range. (I’d just seen You Can See Everything a few weeks before.) We come to the movies to see humans was my brain-rot thought, in the style of Nicole Kidman’s famous AMC commercial. (Brain rot was Oxford’s 2024 Word of the Year.).

Industry observers note that I think back to when it all began. The day after Valentine’s Day last year, my friend Tran casually texted me, asking, “You get into this guy?” with a Spotify link to an album called Heavy Metal by someone called Cameron Winter. I couldn’t tell what it would sound like just by looking at the cover, which was a close-up of his face, criss-crossed by silver chains, but what I soon found were songs dominated by a deep baritone voice and a sweet, jangly guitar or a kind of hazily sensual piano. Who was this guy? Well, it turned out he was the lead singer of this band called Geese—not to be confused with Goose—which he’d started when he was a teen with his high school friends. He’d made this album (jokingly rumored to have been recorded in Guitar Centers, from which he was now banned) and released it without any fanfare that previous December, against the advice of people who knew him and thought the record was too strange or would somehow interfere with the planned Geese release in the newly introduced year. (That album, Getting Killed, was released in September 2025 and turned the band from little-known Brooklyn musicians into both “saviors of rock & roll” and “music label psy-ops,” topping off numerous best-of lists and garnering multiple Grammy nominations.) But none of that had happened yet.

It has been revealed that as I sat in the movie theater, I wondered how many of us in the audience had also been at the performance. What were we looking for in a recording of something we had experienced firsthand? That night, Winter emerged on stage and sat at the piano, his back turned to us. We watched his head sink beneath his shoulders as if he was searching for something deeper inside the instrument, or maybe he was becoming one with it. We had no choice but to completely give ourselves to the music. But Anderson’s camera was nimble and dug itself in other places: a peephole on the stage that looked out to Winter in the foreground and the ocean of people behind him, indeed turning the whole affair into a kind of landscape, swooping in from the audience to Winter at the piano like a detective looking for the culprit of an unnamed crime, or training his lens on the oversize shadow cast by Winter over the audience sitting stage left. I think, “Oh, this is like a musical Rashomon.”.

Industry observers note that during “Drinking Age,” as he sings, “Today, I met who I’m gonna be / from now on / and he’s a piece of shit,” the screen goes dark blue, with only his faint silhouette visible, the weight of his words carrying a brief silence so that you sit there in the emotion. Other times, we experience through Anderson’s POV, seeing the ushers open the backstage doors so that he can step onstage, deftly twirling the camera around Winter’s body. This time he is singing “$0.” It’s perhaps the best song on the album (or at least according to this writer), where he sings with wild abandon, “God is real / God is real / I’m not kidding, God is actually real I’m not kidding this time / I think God is actually for real …” Anderson trains his camera on one of the dramatic light fixtures at the concert hall, a round disc that resembles the sun, then he pans to the audience, then to Winter, small on stage, confessing his small miracle. Afterward, as if exhausted, he delicately plays a simple riff on the piano, while there’s a close-up of his face on screen with heavenly rays of light reflected on his face. I believed him when I first heard it on the album, and I believed him twice more as I heard him sing it live.

Winter stands up; the show is over. The lights come up, and the crowd rises to its feet. I can’t remember now if there was an encore, though I do remember we stood there applauding for a very long time, emotionally drained but joyful that we’d been witnesses. On the screen, the credits roll over images of the crowd, and the two teen girls sitting to my right have spotted themselves in the audience, elated. Winter comes back out for two more songs.

Industry observers note that the movie ends. “Cameron Winter. Live at Carnegie Hall. Dead at 23,” flashes on the screen. Inside the movie theater, the people applaud. I’m still thinking of Winter singing of “com[ing] down to see / my private ceremonies / All on the floor of this room,” and I think, yes, we’re all here in ceremony—or are we in communion?—with one another. The human need for human connection, for human revelations.

Industry observers note that for the occasion, Bahnsen spent half a year designing the collection and also collaborated with her friend Fumiko Imano, the artist, to shoot the campaign in Sweden amidst a picturesque landscape. “It was very much about sisterhood, the journey you do of exploring together, and inspiration also from when I’m in the countryside with my son, and we collect flowers, and how we kind of, he sometimes pinned them on his jumper,” Bahnsen tells ELLE of the new collection. “I think it was really kind of that romantic or nostalgic feeling that I wanted to put into the collection. She’s already been wearing it herself for countryside outings. “There’s romance and nostalgia to pink, and I think with this collaboration, it was nice to do the fleece in pink,” she says. “Showing that it could have that femininity to it was special, and it is also that right tone as a super soft pink that I love.”.

Sources indicate that the entire collection is designed to be layered, and the fleece is at the center of it. There’s a cropped fleece vest, a sheer long T-shirt printed with subtle bouquets of flowers, a floral-embellished fleece skirt and matching socks, gloves, and hats. Bahnsen herself recommends taking a cue from her own runway indicates. “I always love a massive jumper or a big fleece over a poof-y dress,” she says. “It has both a super boyish vibe to it but also a princess-y, romantic feeling, too, so I love those kinds of contrasts between each other.”.

It has been revealed that “These are pieces that you want to not just to work for one season, but to be timeless; it’s become about the perfection of these small details that makes it unique and maybe more romantic than what is normally in the Uniqlo collection,” adds Bahnsen. “I feel like the palette has a really Scandinavian winter tone to it, so how do you balance this soft pink into the darker blacks and blues, and kind of build it up, not in a monocomatic way, but really putting the tones and the layering together.” It’s definitely a chicer way to stay warm. The designer’s latest is the ultimate study of form and function.

Plus, since you’re amongst family and friends, the holiday is the perfect excuse to experiment with some new or elevated styles. Think bouncy blowouts and sleek buns that pair perfectly with your favorite fall sweater or half-up styles finished with velvet bows for a lil holiday flair. Ahead, the cutest Thanksgiving hairstyles to screenshot now. I promise these are quick, effortless, and totally chic, so they won’t take you away from your food, football, or family for too long.

According to recent reports, there’s nothing quite as classic as a major, bouncy blowout. Use a round brush and hair dryer or a blow dryer blush of your choice to get these voluminous waves à la Sabrina Carpenter. This big, glossy volume looks especially great with a fall sweater.

It has been revealed that A festive accessory makes a simple style feel so special. Channel your inner J.Lo with this sleek half-up, half-down look, finished off with a velvet bow to get in the holiday spirit.

Industry observers note that take a cue from Olivia Dean and let your natural curls do the talking this Thanksgiving. These voluminous ringlets are equal parts effortless and glamorous. Recent findings suggest that ponytails are great, but give the classic look a playful upgrade with a bubble braid that’s cute and easy to recreate. Simply secure your hair into a ponytail, add elastics every few inches, and gently tug each section out to create the bubble effect. It’s a fun, trendy option for Thanksgiving that keeps your hair out of your face.

Leave it to Anya Taylor-Joy to make a simple braid look totally elegant. This low side braid proves that you don’t need an elaborate updo to make a statement. Braid your hair loosely on one side and secure with an elastic—you can opt for a discreet clear one for a subtle finish, add an elastic in a autumnal shade for a more festive finish, or really go all out by clipping a bow on the end. According to recent reports, hailey Bieber can make even the seemingly simplest hairstyle look super chic, and her flippy bob is no exception. Channel her style with a retro-inspired sleek bob with ends that flip outward for some extra movement. Recreate the look with a round brush and blow-dryer or a flat iron, curling the ends away from your face.

It has been revealed that why settle for one braid when you can have two? Double braided ponytails are a playful way to switch up your Thanksgiving hairstyle. The how-to is simple: Split your ponytail into two pieces and braid each length separately.

Sources indicate that effortlessly cool, a half-up, half-down hairstyle is proof that sometimes less really is more. It’s the perfect balance between polished and undone, keeping hair away from the face while letting the rest of the lengths flow freely. It’s an especially chic and easy option for Thanksgiving dinner that’s Zoe Kravitz-approved.

In a recent development, nobody does quiet luxury beauty quite like Sofia Richie Grainge, and her signature slicked-back low bun is the definition of understated elegance. It’s sophisticated, timeless, and practically guaranteed to survive the whole night, from appetizers to dinner to dessert.

Bella Hadid may be the face of Saint Laurent and Prada, and she may own every high-profile runway she’s on, but her long-term life goal doesn’t involve spotlights or mega fame. In her fresh cover story for Harper’s Bazaar, the supermodel opens up like never before about what she sees for her future.

In a recent development, “From an external space, success is about how known you are, how much you make, how many times you can be on TV, how many covers you’re on, how many fashion highlights you do. And that is really crucial in our industry, especially when you’re building,” she notes. “But for me, I am different.”.

While she feels endlessly lucky for her place in the fashion industry, and admits that having opened the Victoria’s Secret fashion show last month was a dream come true, she yearns for an easy life surrounded by family and nature.

“Success, for me, can be living in peace, in a small town, with a man that I love, with my child, having my animals,” Hadid notes.

A cowgirl at heart, the Orebella founder has down-to-earth goals that do not necessarily involve modeling, but do involve having a small local business, leaning into hobbies that bring her peace, and becoming a wife and mother.

“I’ve always wanted to start a farm-to-table bakery, with flowers, and everything comes from the community. I want to do things that are fulfilling for me in my soul: having a greenhouse that I can garden in, having my glassblowing and ceramic studio, and having lots of children and being a mother,” she indicates. “It wasn’t a dream that I’ve always had, but it’s something that now is so intense for me. My intuition is screaming so loudly at me about it.”.

Azzedine Alaïa Changed Fashion on His Own Terms

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the 1980s, Azzedine Alaïa acquired a title that followed him for the rest of his career: the “King of Cling.” The moniker was a fitting one: the Tunisian couturier was renowned for his sculptural, body-centric designs. He experimented with stretch jersey and “anti-stress” fibers to sculpt the body without restricting movement.

Sources indicate that but the nickname was also limiting, failing to capture the full scope of his work. The first major U.S. retrospective devoted to Alaïa, “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor, brings his broader legacy into focus through 80 garments and selections from his personal collection of historic fashion.

“As my research went on, I came to realize how notable the U.S. market was in Alaïa’s launch,” Laura L. Camerlengo, co-curator of the exhibit and curator in charge of Costume and Textile Arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, tells ELLE. “By the [brand’s] third season, the U.S. was the second highest market after France, [with interest from] both luxury department stores and small independent retailers.”.

The exhibition took shape after Camerlengo reached out to Olivier Saillard, director of the Fondation Azzedine Alaïa in Paris, who became her co-curator. As visitors enter the Legion of Honor’s Rosekrans Court, they encounter a dress designed for Grace Jones: a spring/summer 1986 haute couture look that Jones modeled on the runway and wore to the 1985 Oscars de la Mode. Part of the opening display, titled “The Women Who Made Alaïa,” it sets the tone for a show that recognizes the muses—both famous and private clients—who wore and supported his work.

Also on view are looks made famous by Rihanna—namely, a sheer red halter gown with a flowing train that she wore to the 2013 Grammys—and Tina Turner, whose silk-organza dress embroidered with gold-tone beads from Alaïa’s spring/summer 1989 concludes the exhibition.

The show then turns to Alaïa’s iconography, as Camerlengo puts it: the bandage dress, his work in denim, and zippered dresses, as well as rare, lesser-seen gems. “I was really keen to have early works on view, particularly the pieces from the 1980s, when he was launching his brand,” the curator states. “These are pieces that would have been shown at Bergdorf Goodman when he had his first fashion show in the United States.”.

The exhibition also places Alaïa’s designs in conversation with the museum’s permanent collection. Belle Epoque-style ensembles from his spring/summer 1992 collection appear among 18th-century European paintings and furnishings, including a Canaletto view of Venice and a sofa commissioned for Marie Antoinette.

Alaïa’s own collection of historic fashion, previously shown in the 2023 Paris exhibition “Azzedine Alaïa, couturier collectionneur,” is represented here, too. The gallery includes pieces by fashion houses he admired, such as Lanvin, Chanel, Balenciaga, and Schiaparelli.

Industry observers note that though Alaïa, who died in 2017 at age 82, is remembered for the body-conscious designs that earned him that “King of Cling” title, he was also a renegade in an industry built around constant production. He revealed collections only when he felt they were ready—a maverick approach that still resonates today—and had his creations worn by a who’s who of the modeling world, from Naomi Campbell to Gisele Bündchen. Many of his designs were featured in the pages of ELLE over the decades.

“He was someone who pioneered a latest way of thinking about fashion,” Camerlengo says. “He was one of the first to question the fashion system and seasonal calendars and the need for trends. He was focused on meticulous craftsmanship and intentionality in design, a sort of precedent to what we think about today, where we are critical of overproduction and overconsumption in fashion.”.

It has been revealed that “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion” is on view at the Legion of Honor Museum from Nov. 21, 2026, to Apr. 11, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the best things to come out of Dancing With the Stars season 35? After Guillermo Rodriguez’s assisted knee walks and the chaotic Cat in the Hat dance routine following Tyler Cameron’s baby gender reveal, it’s got to be Ezra Frech and Connor Wood’s unexpected bromance.

In a recent development, despite premiering over 21 years ago, the show is right now experiencing a major modern resurgence, and social media engagement is to thank. The show has tapped into younger audiences both with its casting choices and through daily behind-the-scenes clips, to the point where even A-listers like Jennifer Lawrence can recognize Connor drinking a smoothie on the street. (By the way, if you’re wondering whether J. Law has reached out to him since he paid her no mind, the answer is sadly no. “I beat that horse to death,” Connor notes. “I’m sure she’s like, ‘Can this guy let it go?’”).

In a recent development, and it’s also thanks to social media that fans have gotten a front-row seat to Connor and Ezra’s off-camera bond. What began with a TikTok poking fun at the fact that Connor’s nickname is Fibula and Ezra was born without his left fibula (which was all Ezra’s idea, according to Connor) has blossomed into an iconic friendship. Now, the besties must face off as the two remaining male stars heading into the finale—but they’re not going to let a little competition come between them.

Sources indicate that “Ezra is definitely more competitive,” Connor, who’s paired with Rylee Arnold, tells Cosmopolitan. “He’s got a fighting spirit. When we get to eliminations, I’m thinking about my post-show quesadilla. I mean, obviously I want to stay in the competition. But I’ve considered every week that I’ve made it a win. The only person I’m competitive with is myself because I want to get this right.”.

“This is a competition show, but you’re kind of rooting for everybody else and want everyone else to do well,” Ezra, who’s partnered with Daniella Karagach, adds. “Plus, there’s so much that’s out of your control. I want Connor to succeed. He wants me to succeed. You know, it’s real love.”.

The first time the two met was at the promo photo shoot ahead of the season premiere, where the connection was so instantaneous that Connor thought they must already know each other. As Connor explains, “We’re hugging, we’re chatting, and then I’m walking away like, ‘Oh my gosh, where did I meet him before?’ Turns out, it was our first time meeting. We just connected straight off the bat.”.

In a recent development, “Sometimes you’ll meet somebody and just click and know like, ‘Oh, that’s somebody I’m gonna be friends with,’” says Ezra of that fateful first meeting. “I’m sure Connor and I would have definitely hit it off and become really close in any other context—but I think Dancing With the Stars accelerated that timeline because we’re both way out of our comfort zone. For us to be in this together, it’s bonded us in a very unique way.”.

Industry observers note that they may be a decade apart in age (Connor is 31 as of September, while Ezra was born a month before DWTS first premiered in 2005) and come from two entirely different worlds (Connor is a podcaster and comedian, while Ezra is a two-time Paralympian with two gold medals to prove it), but their friendship? From post-rehearsal dance parties to spray tan dates to trailer talks, it knows no bounds.

Cosmopolitan caught up with Ezra and Connor ahead of the DWTS season 35 finale to chat about beating the odds, blocking out the noise, and what happens after they leave the ballroom.

Connor: I thought there was more to the sentence. I thought I would hear, “Connor and Rylee, come down here and dance for us again.” I literally walked backstage after they called mine and Rylee’s name, and I took off my jacket and just sat on the ground. I was in shock.

Ezra: They do say names are called in no particular order, but when I was standing there with Harry [Shum Jr.], I was just like, “Wow, this is crazy.” No one will tell you that they’re standing up there feeling confident, so when they leave you up there longer, it definitely makes you sweat.

Connor: I’m an extrovert, but it’s very selective. I don’t do emotions. Being on the show, I’ve put out a more vulnerable me. I’ve been sharing things on national TV that I don’t even share with my friends, and it’s been wildly uncomfortable in the best way. You know, I’ve always found work for myself that’s come really easy to me—like, comedy has been natural for me. This is nothing like that. This is the hardest I’ve ever worked in my life, and my brain chemistry has been changed forever because of this.

Ezra: I didn’t come in with any dance experience, and quite frankly, I thought I had natural limitations on what I was capable of on the dance floor. What Dani has brought out of me is almost rewiring the limitations I placed on myself and changing my own expectations of what I can do on a prosthetic—which is crazy, because I’ve lived 21 years and felt like I had a pretty good understanding of what I was capable of on my own prosthetic leg. Then I come on Dancing With the Stars and meet Dani and that completely shifts.

Connor: [laughs] You think I’m watching myself? Oh, no. I don’t watch. And the choreo has been hard, but it’s gotten easier each week for me to learn dances. Like, learning the week 3 samba, I’m like, “Rylee, pack your bags. It’s been great getting to know you.” But now I know that I’ll get it.

Sources indicate that ezra: Yeah, I don’t really watch. I mean, I end up seeing clips, and earlier in the season, I would rewatch the dances. But everything’s happening so fast; it’s hard to, like, really sit and marinate on them when you gotta refocus for the next week. The cool thing is these dances will live forever. They’re out there in the world, and I will be able to watch and appreciate those moments and have pride in them for the rest of my life.

Recent findings suggest that connor: Michael Scott noted it best: “Do I need to be liked? Absolutely not. I like to be liked. I enjoy being liked. I have to be liked.” I relate to that so much, because I’ll want to reach out to someone and be like, “Do you really hate me? Like, walk me through what I did during my jive that has made you just despise me?” I don’t think these people actually have that much hatred in their heart. I think they’re really invested fans, and it’s part of the game. Would I slide into someone’s DMs and say, “Watch your back”? No. But I know it’s what I signed up for.

Ezra: People online—as far as whether they think you’re great or mediocre or suck or whatever the opinions are on social media—shouldn’t influence your day-to-day. Thankfully, for Dani and I, there haven’t been too many negative comments, but, of course, with every 30 positive comments, you’re going to get a negative comment. It’s all about not letting that little negative comment overshadow the beautiful stuff that people are saying online as well.

Connor: This is a once-in-a-lifetime chance, but it’s also objectively fun. It’s a show about dancing. I’m not going to make a joke of it, but there’s humor involved. It’s so notable to take a step back and laugh sometimes. This is fun. It should be fun.

It has been revealed that connor: You do it anxious. You know, there are people like Ezra with serious uphill battles, and he’s crushing it. I’m just here with anxiety and ADHD and small amounts of OCD and dancing on TV. It’s just something that I’ve always dealt with. I go into standup anxious, and honestly, I think it helps me operate. It pushes me to make sure I get in all of my rehearsal hours so that there’s nothing to be anxious about. As my dad told me, “If you weren’t anxious, you would be anxious.”.

Ezra: I think the way we phrase things in our head controls the way we feel about them. Yes, it can be a burden to feel like you’re representing a community, but it’s a beautiful burden, and so I don’t see it as a negative thing. I get to play a small role in representing my community on such a special show like Dancing With the Stars—I think it’s actually, like, the pride and joy and honor of my life.

Ezra: No, it’s not in my DNA to chill. I mean, after 2028, I’ll probably take some downtime for sure—but then, you know, you’ve got the next Games in 2032, you’ve got world championships the next year, so there’s never really an end. I’ll probably compete on the track for another 15 years or so. And hopefully after the show ends, I’ll take a nice vacation or just rot for a little bit.

It has been revealed that connor: Rylee and Ezra are the same age, and you know, I do feel my age a lot of the time when I talk to them. Like, Rylee only knew who Nicole Kidman was because of the AMC pre-roll ads, and Ezra hadn’t seen High School Musical when we were doing the Wildcats dance. But both of them are so wise beyond their years. As soon as Ezra and I became friends, I started seeing old clips of him at, like, 9 years old on Ellen, and he was probably more eloquent and emotionally mature than I am now. People keep wanting him to be the Bachelor, but I think he needs to run for office. He’s just got this natural charisma.

According to recent reports, ezra: I didn’t listen to his podcast, but I’d seen clips of him online, and I knew of him. There’s a really funny video of a Team USA thing that I did two or three years ago where I’m lip-syncing to Connor’s audio. It’s like, “I have purse; I have shoe.” And now people are like, “Wow, the invisible string theory brought them together.” It’s funny; he’s the exact same online versus in person. He’s the same dude. He’s able to take things in, he’s able to feel them, and then he’s able to articulate them in a way that resonates with people. That’s what makes him so good as a comedian.

According to recent reports, connor: There’s this guy in a suit that’s jumping straight up in the air and it looks like an exclamation point. I’d say that’s Ezra, since he’s so elevated in the way he carries himself. And, of course, he’s got hops.

Industry observers note that ezra: I would describe Connor with the emoji that’s smiling and sweating, because he’s always smiling and he’s always kind of sweating, and it’s sort of perfect. Like, he’ll make jokes and then look around like, “Ooh, did that land?”.

According to recent reports, connor: Val [Chmerkovskiy] and Jenna [Johnson] and I are gonna work on hip-hop dance at their studio. Val and I are also doing a standup show together at some point. I just adore Brandon [Armstrong] and Alan [Bersten], too. Us three together? Trouble. Britt [Stewart] and I connected on some zen woo-woo stuff, so we’re gonna hang out. And Jenna Dewan and her partner Steve [Kazee], we’re gonna hang out. Julianne [Hough] and I are gonna hang out in Upcoming York. I mean, I talk to everybody. I hope I see everybody again.

In a recent development, ezra: Amber [Glenn] is someone who is a real close part of my life and will be for a long time. I feel like her and I are on the same team together in this with Pasha [Pashkov] and Dani. Guillermo is someone I’m going to be close to forever. Like me, him, and Connor—we’re in the group chat texting all the time. And I love Tyler Cameron, and Harry is the sweetest, and Jenna—like, it’s hard to pick and choose. I could see myself still talking to pretty much everybody on the cast.

Ezra: The internet is crazy. Right now, I’m definitely single but not necessarily looking for a relationship. Because, again, once the dance season ends, I’ll be committing myself entirely to track again. I’m enjoying being single, and it’ll probably stay that way for a while.

According to recent reports, connor: This has been like a study abroad trip. Like, I am fully immersed in a culture that is so far outside of my comfort zone and so far away from what I know. Learning something new at my age is so rare, let alone at this level on TV with a world-class athlete teaching me. And if it does happen, it probably happens to billionaires’ kids who are, like, paying Serena Williams to do private lessons for two years. I think I’m gonna wake up on Wednesday feeling like I walked out of a loud party and shut the door with my ears still ringing. Like, I’m alone. Party is over. It’s time to go home.

According to recent reports, ezra: I’ll miss getting to see everyone at the rehearsal studio. I’ll miss getting lunch with Dani after practice. I’ll miss getting the opportunity to commit myself to something like this so entirely. And I’m gonna miss the show days. You become so close to everybody, and you spend so much time around these people, and then all of a sudden, it’s going to end. But the good thing is that these people are still going to be in my life. I’m still going to hang out with Dani, and I’m still going to see Connor whenever I can, and we’ll get lunch with Guillermo. These are people I’ll be with forever.

Tech Report: How to Care for a Thanksgiving Cactus so It Blooms Right on Time

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want an easy-care plant to brighten your home through fall and winter?
  • Thanksgiving cacti can grow outdoors in USDA Hardiness Zones 10–12, but they’re well suited to indoor life in any climate.
  • Sources indicate that wondering how to help yours thrive?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want an easy-care plant to brighten your home through fall and winter? Skip the usual mums and try a Thanksgiving cactus. Though it’s native to Brazil, this plant looks nothing like a desert cactus: Its flat, toothed stems end in pointed tips, and its vivid tubular flowers usually appear in late November. That timing is how it got its name. It’s related to Easter and Christmas cacti, which flower around their namesake holidays.

Thanksgiving cacti can grow outdoors in USDA Hardiness Zones 10–12, but they’re well suited to indoor life in any climate. Their bright flowers come in colors including red, pink, white, and yellow, adding a cheerful burst of color to a room.

Sources indicate that wondering how to help yours thrive? Here’s what to know about growing and caring for a Thanksgiving cactus.

The Thanksgiving cactus loves bright spots that aren't in direct sunlight. Too much sun can cause the plant to turn yellow rather than its beautiful green, so keeping it by a north- or east-facing window or even a shady south- or west-facing window is ideal. For your plant to produce the best flowers, it shouldn't receive more than 12 hours of light. It needs the darkness to produce blooms.

Recent findings suggest that all holiday cacti require a bit more magnesium than other houseplants, so finding your Thanksgiving cactus a magnesium-rich fertilizer you can add to a well-draining soil is essential. The Home and Garden Information Center (HGIC) suggests supplementing its water with Epsom salts—try mixing in one teaspoon of Epsom salts per gallon of water. But avoid doing so during the week you add the fertilizer, which you should do once a month. Stop adding fertilizer in the late summer months for better flower production in the fall.

Sources indicate that thanksgiving cacti should be planted in a pot with drainage holes at the bottom since they won't thrive in soggy soil. Consider adding peat moss or sand to the pot to prevent pooling water around the roots. Thanksgiving cacti are root-bound, so there's no need to repot them for about two to three years.

Sources indicate that the soil surrounding your Thanksgiving cactus should never be soaking wet or bone dry. However, the soil should be consistently moist and never fully dry to the touch. Holiday cacti are prone to root rot, so standing water is your main enemy. During the hot months, they can stand to be slightly underwatered.

Like most tropical plants, Thanksgiving cacti thrive in a humid, warm environment. However, the typical household temperature can keep a cactus very healthy too. The temperature shouldn't get above 80 degrees Fahrenheit or below 55 degrees, though ideally you should keep your cactus between 75 and 80 degrees during the day, according to the University of Wisconsin-Madison's Horticulture Department.

Recent findings suggest that pruning is an important task for plant lovers to keep any houseplant healthy, and Thanksgiving cacti are no different. To promote bud growth, cut the stems in the late spring or early summer, and make sure you have the right gardening tools for the job. Be sure to save the cut stems for propagation too!

Industry observers note that if you want more of these tropical cacti around your house, maybe for a huge, flowering centerpiece for the holidays, use cut stems to produce more plants. HGIC suggests using stems with three to five phylloclades (or stem joints) on each to start. Set the segments aside for a day to dry out, then stick them about one inch deep into a pot with moist soil. Do this only in the spring and summer while the plant is actively growing, and avoid doing it in the winter once it has bloomed.

Because the Thanksgiving cactus is native to Brazil, you should try to mimic its natural environment as best you can to get it to bloom, which is near the end of the rainy season. The gardening department at Michigan State University Extension explains that for the buds to develop on your indoor plant, Thanksgiving cacti need at least 13 hours of total darkness each day, bright light when they're not covered up or hidden away, and a consistent temperature ranging between 55 and 65 degrees. You should start this process in late September or early October if you want blooms around the holiday season.

Once the plant has flowered for the season, then you can go back to taking care of it the way you normally would with the help of the guidelines written above.

According to recent reports, according to PetMD, Thanksgiving cacti are not toxic to dogs and cats, unlike another holiday plant, the poinsettia. However, that doesn't mean you should let your furry friends munch on it. If large amounts are consumed, your pets can experience vomiting, diarrhea, and a decreased appetite.
