Sources indicate that casseroles remind me of cuddling up at home by the fire with my loved ones and digging into the tastiest dishes. They're also some of the easiest recipes to throw together in no time, and are the best for serving a holiday crowd. What else could you want? Now that we're firmly in the cold season, I can't stop craving them, so obviously, I turn to my favorite Delish recipes to make it happen. This holiday season, make sure to try out these 12 casserole recipes for some of the best bites you'll have all season. We have some classics, like a comforting chicken and rice casserole that'll have you dreaming of home, alongside more inventive and mouthwatering dishes like our French onion croissant strata.

It has been revealed that there are few pairings as classic as meatloaf and mashed potatoes, but this casserole is anything but basic. Take your side of mashed potatoes, stack it on top of your meatloaf, and load it up with all of your favorite baked potato toppings. You’ll have an indulgent, craveable casserole that turns into the best leftovers—if you have any.

When you’re hungry for something that’s comforting, cozy, and a little luxe feeling too, chicken Marsala is a truly excellent option. The pan sauce has plenty of mushrooms, fortified Marsala wine, and a splash of cream, because why not? It’s a fantastic dinner, easy enough for a weeknight and special enough for date night.

In a recent development, A breakfast strata is one of our go-tos when we want a hearty, shareable brunch dish, but it’s hard to put into words how good this French onion croissant strata is. It takes a few extra minutes to deeply caramelize the onions, but the extra flavor and richness make a HUGE difference.

Chicken soup is a comfort food icon, good for the soul and the stomach, and there are a world’s worth of chicken soup recipes to choose from. Take chicken, egg noodles, some veggies, and a creamy sauce and bake them into a hearty casserole? You have a hearty dinner that leads to full bellies and happy hearts.

Slow-Cooker Cowboy Potato Casserole.

This slow-cooker casserole, featuring potatoes, beans, corn, and lots of cheese, is hearty, packed with flavor, and sure to make repeat appearances on your grub rotation all fall long.

Chicken and broccoli casserole is a meal that most people at Team Delish grew up eating, and this recipe is guaranteed to make you feel like a kid again. This creamy, cheesy, Ritz cracker-topped casserole is packed with chicken, rice, and freshly blanched broccoli with the quintessential cream of mushroom soup.

Apple Cheddar Crescent Casserole.

It has been revealed that when it comes to this casserole, think breakfast strata with buttery, caramelized apples, and lots of sharp cheddar. If you’re in need of a quick fall-forward recipe to throw together for a weekend brunch, you can easily turn to this one.

When we need a direct flight to a quick and easy dinner destination, we turn to two trusty options: a casserole or a chicken dinner. This chicken and rice casserole is the best of both worlds. It requires minimal cleanup, and the hands-on cooking time is only 20 minutes. The rest of the time, you can just lounge in your living room while this whips itself up.

It has been revealed that when the weather gets cold, your dinner making-mojo is low, or when comfort food is just what’s on the menu, you need a casserole. Even though we have loved so many other casseroles before, there's always room in my baking dish for one more. And if that casserole is easy, creamy, chicken-y, and cheesy? With a crunchy topping? Our oven is already preheating.

In a recent development, watch out, classic green bean casserole, gnocchi has entered the holiday menu. We took the classic recipe and added gnocchi for a dish that's infinitely better than the sum of its parts. Blanched fresh green beans and buttery sliced mushrooms, onions, and garlic get tossed with a creamy béchamel sauce and pillowy gnocchi, then baked until bubbly.

This enchilada casserole is what weeknight dinner dreams are made of. Classic chicken enchiladas are a fan-favorite meal, but they can be kind of tedious to prepare when you're low on energy (all that rolling, right?). In this recipe, you just layer all your components in a casserole dish, bake until melty and saucy, add your desired toppings, and serve!

In our book, it doesn't get more comforting than shepherd's pie. Because this meat and potatoes dish is such a classic, we spent a while perfecting the comfort food staple—your weeknights should be as cozy as possible.

  • While scrolling through my Instagram feed last week, I came across a pair of T-shirts made by Sofia Coppola for Mack Books.
  • But it also got me thinking, not for the first time, about film directors and fashion.
  • But it’s also partly why the best directors—those who spend their lives building worlds and poring over the details of what their character might say, do, and, most importantly for our purposes, wear—have become as compelling to watch on the red carpet as the contract-bound movie stars they direct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While scrolling through my Instagram feed last week, I came across a pair of T-shirts made by Sofia Coppola for Mack Books. To celebrate the release of her mother Eleanor’s documentary, Making Marie Antoinette—a portrait compiled from archival footage shot during the making of Coppola’s 2006 cult classic—as well as the original film’s 20th anniversary, Coppola has released a limited-edition capsule collection printed with on-set photography by Andrew Durham. Naturally, I had a T-shirt in my basket faster than you could say “Let them eat cake.” (In case you were wondering, I went for the one with Kirsten Dunst looking wistfully out from a rococo horse-drawn carriage, a camera rig looming in the foreground.).

But it also got me thinking, not for the first time, about film directors and fashion. There’s a reason why the behind-the-scenes photos from that movie—Dunst and Jason Schwartzman in powdered wigs and full Versailles regalia listening to their iPods, Coppola crouched behind a monitor in a button-down and jeans; you know the ones—have remained such an enduring touchstone within the online cultural consciousness, from Tumblr to TikTok. There’s something both fascinating and lightly absurd about the friction between the practical, gorpy clothing worn by most on a film set and the breathtaking opulence of the period costuming. And in Making Marie Antoinette, Coppola’s casual but stylish on-set wardrobe of well-cut mid-aughts basics is, counterintuitively, almost as captivating as Milena Canonero’s glorious 18th-century costume confections. Which I guess is partly why Coppola made those T-shirts.

But it’s also partly why the best directors—those who spend their lives building worlds and poring over the details of what their character might say, do, and, most importantly for our purposes, wear—have become as compelling to watch on the red carpet as the contract-bound movie stars they direct. (It’s little wonder that some of history’s greatest filmmakers were also some of history’s most stylish, possessing an innate understanding of the storytelling power of clothes: Agnès Varda, David Lynch, Wong Kar-wai, the list goes on.).

Which brings me to the 2026 awards trail—and the 2027 awards trail, which is now kicking into gear—where the sartorial approaches have been refreshingly eclectic. While promoting Sinners, Ryan Coogler’s killer red carpet looks included a three-piece Thom Browne suit with a diamond brooch at the Golden Globes, a slouchy Fear of God suit at the SAG Awards, and a sharp Louis Vuitton tux at the Oscars.

Ryan Coogler (with his wife, Zinzi) in Thom Browne at the Golden Globes.

Coogler in Louis Vuitton at the Oscars.

Recent findings suggest that for Chloé Zhao—who, not coincidentally, earned a spot on this year’s Vogue best dressed list—campaigning for Hamnet appeared to involve taking cues from the world of her film. (Turns out directors can do method dressing too.) Working with Gabriela Hearst, she wore a gold gown with a Tudor-inflected Basque waist at the BAFTAs, while at the Academy Awards, she wore a headline-grabbing gown inspired by Victorian mourning dress—complete with draped bell sleeves, Bulgari diamonds, and a sheer black veil—that she described as “the alchemical image of the crow.” Try getting that level of commitment from a leading man in a black tux and a brand-deal watch.

Chloé Zhao in Gabriela Hearst at the BAFTAs.

Zhao in Gabriela Hearst at the Oscars.

Industry observers note that thankfully, this year, there’s a latest crop of fashion-fluent directors ready to take up the mantle. Just take Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known collectively as Los Javis, who have happily matched the maximalist, operatic sweep of their Lorca-inspired epic La Bola Negra with their steady stream of playful tailoring—coordinating Loewe suits at the Biarritz Film Festival, say, or oversized shirting and denim to the Chanel show over the summer—proving their flair for the visual extends well beyond the silver screen.

Los Javis—or Javi Ambrossi and Javi Calvo—at the GQ Men of the Year Awards in Madrid.

Ambrossi and Calvo in Chanel at the brand’s haute couture fall 2026 show.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Olivia Wilde has been delivering some of the year’s sharpest high-low looks while promoting The Invite—everything from a custom Saint Laurent dress with an ab-baring cutout at the Los Angeles premiere, to a boxy black vintage tee and double-pleated pants from The Row for a SAG-AFTRA event. “I really love not having to dress up in the same way as I have as an actress,” she told Chloe Malle on the Vogue podcast earlier this year. “I do feel like after decades of tarting myself up for press tours, I am so relieved to be like, ‘You know what? They wear T-shirts. I’m gonna wear a fucking T-shirt.’” (Granted, wearing a T-shirt hits a little differently when it’s tucked into pants that cost roughly the same as a secondhand Honda Civic, but the point stands.).

Olivia Wilde in Saint Laurent at The Invite’s Los Angeles premiere.

Wilde in a vintage x Karla tee and The Row pants at a SAG-AFTRA Foundation event.

Then, there’s Greta Gerwig, who’s gearing up for the February release of her rock-opera-inspired Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew, whose looks this year—Bottega Veneta, Stella McCartney, Diotima by Rachel Scott—hint at a bold (and largely female-designed) press tour wardrobe to come.

Greta Gerwig in Bottega Veneta at the PGA Awards.

Gerwig in Ashlyn at the opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art.

Industry observers note that and finally, for a new vanguard of filmmakers, the press tour has become a place to subvert the traditional codes of men’s tailoring. On that front, there’s Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman and the Bottega Veneta suit he wore for the Los Angeles premiere, with its oversized powder-pink collar peeking over the top of the lapels, or the Tom Ford by Haider Ackermann jacket for the New York premiere that featured a silk floral boutonnière with a flowing ribbon. Or Jane Schoenbrun, who debuted their queer slasher, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, in Cannes with a series of offbeat looks that included a particularly delightful puffball skirt suit with powder-blue tights and Mary Janes.

Jordan Firstman in Tom Ford by Haider Ackermann at the Latest York premiere of Club Kid.

Jane Schoenbrun at the Cannes premiere of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.

Sources indicate that it helps, of course, that in 2026, the lines between luxury fashion houses and cinema have all but dissolved. Fashion is no longer just dressing actors and directors for the premiere, or awards show; it’s actively financing, producing, and inserting itself into their work. In September, Dior unveiled a two-year creative partnership with A24 before doubling down just this week with a new Sundance Institute fellowship supporting women filmmakers. The Anthony Vaccarello–founded Saint Laurent Productions has cemented itself as a Cannes and awards-season powerhouse, backing auteurs such as Jim Jarmusch and Claire Denis. And some designers are stepping into the film set trenches, too—most notably Jonathan Anderson, who followed up his work on Challengers and Queer by designing the costumes for Guadagnino’s hotly anticipated Silicon Valley satire Artificial.

Sources indicate that clothes maketh the man. All of these directors know that clothes maketh the character. So let’s hope that, this awards season, clothes continue to maketh the filmmaker, too—and if they ever run out of ideas, I’ve got a Marie Antoinette T-shirt they’re welcome to borrow.

It has been revealed that thanksgiving is a beautiful time with family, but just like figuring out how to fit all your loved ones around the dinner table, you're also bound to struggle to find space in your oven for all the amazing foods you want to cook. By the time you’ve made your roasted turkey, stuffing, green bean casserole, and sweet potato casserole with marshmallows, there’s no more space or time left for dessert. The Delish team is here to say we’ve got dessert covered —and it requires *zero* time in the oven, so you won’t have to play oven Jenga with all your delicious Thanksgiving sides. These 24 dessert recipes won’t take up an inch of that coveted oven space.

Looking for more easy Thanksgiving recipe ideas? Check out our easy last-minute Thanksgiving recipe ideas!

It has been revealed that pumpkin pie spice, vanilla pudding, and fresh pumpkin puree are whipped into a light and fluffy dip that’s not as heavy as the classic fall pie, yet still has all of the festive flavors you love. Thanks to this dip, you can have pumpkin pie for dessert and as an appetizer—pumpkin pie 24/7!

This Thanksgiving, step out of your culinary comfort zone and embrace the future of festive feasting. Make a turkey sculpture out of Rice Krispies treats and watch as your holiday transforms from traditional to extraordinary. Your guests will thank you, your Instagram followers will envy you, and you’ll have a Thanksgiving memory that’s as sweet as it is unforgettable.

Air Fryer Apple Pie Baked Apples.

Better Than Magnolia Bakery Banana Pudding.

Recent findings suggest that after testing and retesting, our better than Magnolia Bakery banana pudding was born. This is a very bold statement, we know. But once you’ve had a spoonful of this version with its from-scratch pudding, perfectly ripe bananas, and luxurious Italian meringue, you’ll understand where we're coming from.

What’s better than scoring a turkey leg at the holiday dinner table? Answer: snagging one of these gooey marshmallow and chocolate Rice Krispies treats formed and shaped to just look like one. 😉.

This over-the-top pumpkin dessert takes 30 minutes to throw together, and once it's assembled, the refrigerator does the rest. Talk about a no-fuss Thanksgiving treat! Crêpe cake is a cool, lofty masterpiece composed of layers of crêpes and lightened vanilla pastry cream, all topped with a billowing cloud of whipped cream and a crown of fresh berries. It’s light, creamy, and absolutely irresistible.

Recent findings suggest that cheesecake bars are always a great option, but when we're looking for a party dessert that no one will expect, we turn to these cheesecake-filled egg rolls. Industry observers note that this chocolate tart is great for a last-minute dessert because it mainly uses store-bought ingredients, and the majority of the time required for this recipe is just letting it chill in the refrigerator. Be patient—it's SO worth it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most people might build an outfit around a pair of shoes. Others, around a jacket. But few, surprisingly, do it around a belt.

Sources indicate that at GQ, we’ve always stated that the overlooked belt is more than the sum of its buckle and holes. Not only will it stop your slacks from going south, but a good leather belt can make just as much of a statement as your shoes, and deliver as much of a stylistic flourish as a tie. Unconvinced? Enter: The studded belt. (Which, coincidentally, we're now increasingly seeing be offered by some of the most imitated brands in the industry, from Lemaire to RRL, Mfpen to Our Legacy.).

In a recent development, the charm of the studded belt is that it’s a vibe chameleon. Its decorative elements can pay tribute to any number of aesthetics, from Americana to punk to European artistry. And while any one will easily provide further flair to an already-singing outfit, the best ones also single-handedly bring even the most minimalist wardrobe to life. (And to be honest, that’s how I feel studded belts are best worn today: Against a white tee and jeans, for an easy win without changing your whole look.).

Industry observers note that to help you find the right one for you, I've sorted through the vast waist-wear market to find a selection that won't just make your outfits sing, but set them on course for superstardom. See you out there, Stud.

Recent findings suggest that let's start gently: Somehow, Anderson’s has made a studded belt that whispers. It’s a small but mighty addition to their lovingly handcrafted Italian leather goods.

“If a stud falls out, make a wish,” is the outlook over at Htc Los Angeles—and they provide plenty of it. A true purveyor of the style, the brand has been specializing in rock-and-roll embellished leather goods since the ’90s. And they aren’t stingy with it either.

It has been revealed that trust Corridor NYC to come in clutch for all of your folksy Americana needs. The worn-in look of their studded belt—made in full-grain leather and tarnished hardware—carries all the tales of someone who’s worn it through the arid badlands.

If the fits over at the Ralph Lauren PoloFest in Tokyo last month have inspired you to join the RL tribe, any one of the many studded belts from RRL (Ralph's ranch-minded line) is a strong place to start.

It has been revealed that as you’ll see from our list, Our Legacy—a staple for any serious fashion guy—has secured two call-outs. Here, they cut diamond studs to form a snakeskin-like pattern that, when worn against your best corduroy pants, gives the look some severe shine.

While we’re talking about studded belts as an easy hardware win, they're also the perfect place to score some color points too. Here, the green and orange mixes it up more than traditional turquoise.

Since its founding in 2012, Maximum Henry has been handmaking our favorite leather goods right here in Upcoming York City, including their beloved oval buckle belt. But they also know how to do a good, uncomplicated studded belt.

In a recent development, the floral studs on this OL belt aren’t merely decorative, but are punched into the very function of the eyelets. It’s a sweet look, really, and one done so effortlessly.

Dressing for winter, when all you ever want to feel is cozy, can leave you feeling like a schlub. There is, however, an easy fix in the form of the enviably Parisian stylings of Lemaire, who’ve released a brown belt with almond-shaped studs. Wear it with your all-denim outfit or heavy grey wool pants, it’ll make you feel like one of the brand’s cityslicking models in their closely-studied runway demonstrates.

In a recent development, while we’ve so far been paying attention to how studs can add some play, texture still plays a key role to make an outfit sing. A Kind of Guise made their turquoise studded belt with a tan nubuck leather.

Lemaire might be better known for their artsy fabrics and drape-y cuts, but their accessories department is a treasure trove too.

According to recent reports, florals can be a lot generally for most guys, but Mfpen uses theirs sparingly on their lean 2cm wide belt. Made in patent brown leather, it also adds a nice formal sheen to a dark winter ensemble.

Sources indicate that we’ve so far seen how studded belts can sway from Americana to minimalist vibes, but we can’t leave out the heavy metal rockers. Heliot Emil shaves off the edges for something more digestible, but still packs enough punch to cut through a monochromatic outfit.

Meet the Stylists Who Shaped Vogue’s Best-Dressed List

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In case you missed it, Vogue’s 2026 best-dressed list has officially arrived—and on it are plenty of well-clad celebrities driving fashion forward.
  • While all of these A-listers come with their own distinct sense of style, their masterful stylists have played an important role in making them true red-carpet stars.
  • Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Kendall Jenner, Carey Mulligan, Greta Lee, Ayo Edebiri.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In case you missed it, Vogue’s 2026 best-dressed list has officially arrived—and on it are plenty of well-clad celebrities driving fashion forward.

While all of these A-listers come with their own distinct sense of style, their masterful stylists have played an important role in making them true red-carpet stars. As they say, “it takes a village”—so let’s pour one out for the amazing fashion minds who help craft all of the glamorous moments.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Kendall Jenner, Carey Mulligan, Greta Lee, Ayo Edebiri.

It has been revealed that styling approach: “My approach is always client-first. It’s vital to me that what they wear on the red carpet feels authentic to who they are.”.

Favored silhouette: “I’m really drawn to silhouettes that feel a little unexpected and challenge convention, but still translate naturally to the red carpet.”.

Signature touch: “A quiet statement.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “A Sophie Buhai teardrop pouch.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Connor Storrie.

In a recent development, styling approach: “I always start with the person rather than the clothes. For me, great styling is about understanding someone’s personality, proportions, and how they carry themselves, then building on that. With Connor, I’ve always drawn heavily on Old Hollywood, particularly the 1920s and 1930s, bringing those references into something that feels contemporary and a little unexpected. I want the clothes to enhance the person rather than overpower them. There’s nothing better than a beautifully executed look that feels completely effortless.”.

Favored silhouette: “I’m really drawn to a strong shoulder, a slightly higher waist, and a beautiful, long, wide-leg trouser. There’s something incredibly flattering and seductive about those proportions. I love the elegance of traditional menswear, but with a slightly louche, almost 1970s sensibility. It’s masculine without feeling rigid, and there’s a real sense of movement and ease to it.”.

According to recent reports, signature touch: “I think my strength is understanding proportion and knowing when to hold back. I’m much more interested in personal style than chasing trends. Sometimes the smallest adjustments to a jacket, the way a trouser falls or how a shirt sits against the body can completely transform a look. I also love finding that balance between classic elegance and a little sex appeal. Nothing should ever feel forced or as though someone’s wearing a costume.”.

Sources indicate that most-pulled accessory: “Pinky rings. I know they’re having a real moment on the red carpet, particularly in menswear, but they’re something I find myself coming back to. Even for Connor’s most recent red carpet at the Academy Museum Gala, convention might suggest wearing just one, but we loved both Tiffany & Co. rings so much that we decided to wear one on each pinky. One was a platinum ring featuring a cat’s-eye alexandrite surrounded by diamonds, while the other was a platinum ring set with a diamond of over eight carats. Two insanely beautiful pieces, and rather than choosing between them, we thought, why not wear both? I love those little moments where you go against the grain. Sometimes breaking an unwritten fashion rule creates something far more interesting and unexpected, and therein lies the fun of styling!”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Teyana Taylor, Colman Domingo.

In a recent development, styling approach: “Firstly, we consider the event and where our client is at that time in their career to decide what feels right for the moment. It’s also dependent on what our clients feel best in—making sure that they feel their truest and most confident self. Then, between the two of us, we also have to have synergy and feel good about a look, which we almost never disagree on.”.

It has been revealed that favored silhouette: “As we like to say—never waste a waist! We always love cinched-in jackets, corsets, and waistlines and are so happy to see them being modernized on both the runway and red carpet at the moment. Right now we are seeing waistlines highlighted through accentuated peplums, exaggerated hips, and snatched bodices.”.

Signature touch: “Jewelry is beyond important to us and always makes a look feel finished. Whether it’s diamonds, colored stones, or metal-based pieces, we love to use jewelry to elevate or put a twist on a look that might otherwise feel expected.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “We always gravitate towards a Christian Louboutin So Kate pump for our female clients, or the Christian Louboutin Ziggissimo heeled boot for our male clients.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Tessa Thompson, Whitney Peak.

Styling approach: “I think about the project, the event, and what we are communicating. But ultimately, I’m thinking about the woman I’m dressing, and what we have established as a fashion identity. And what makes them feel amazing.”.

Industry observers note that favored silhouette: “I’m not sure this defines my approach. When I see a look, it’s more that I connect it to a person. It’s much more organic and romantic than just saying, ‘Minis for spring!’”.

Signature touch: “My signature touch is that my clients look like they all have the best style, and that the clothes never wear them.”.

In a recent development, most-pulled accessory: “I love a mega earring. And a perfect little sack clutch. I just want to be Mrs. Prada!”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Olivia Rodrigo.

Styling approach: “Our approach is rooted in the individuality of each client, creating looks that feel authentic yet unexpected. We love refined and timeless silhouettes but always need a little edge, or elements that aren’t so perfect. Ultimately, we want every look to tell a story, feel effortless, and leave an impression.”.

Recent findings suggest that favored silhouette: “We are really drawn to the two extremes right now—either something incredibly sculpted and structured, or fluid with beautiful draping. How a look moves, especially on the carpet, is so impactful.”.

Signature touch: “Our signature touch is finding the balance between femininity and edge—we love taking something traditionally beautiful and introducing an unexpected element via a shoe, accessory, fabric, or silhouette.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “Our most pulled accessory is often a rare or untraditional shoe! We don’t always use them, but we are obsessed with interesting shoes.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Rebecca Hall, Morgan Spector.

Sources indicate that styling approach: “I always start with the person rather than the clothes. Understanding who they are, what makes them feel confident, and how they want to be perceived is essential. When putting together a look, I’m already considering the final image. The clothes, accessories, and glam all play a part, as does the way the client carries the look, how they pose, and how it’s photographed. The best looks are a creative collaboration between stylist, glam, and the client.”.

Favored silhouette: “Long column silhouette with a strong neckline.”.

Signature touch: “Clean lines with a touch of drama or tension.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “Black pointed toe pumps.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Daisy Edgar-Jones, Kendall Jenner.

According to recent reports, styling approach: “I always say I try to see my client’s style, just through my eyes. It always starts and ends with them, and that excitement when our visions align is when the relationship is magic.”.

Favored silhouette: “Knee-length skirts (even better if it’s a skirt suit), medium-sized bags, and square-toe heels—I can never get enough.”.

Sources indicate that signature touch: “Chic and cool. That combo is always what underwrites my vision. I’m always drawn to looks that say something but are still timeless—that make a moment in one part being really interesting, and the rest being really fluid, classic, or refined.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “Black satin slingback pumps and great sunglasses.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Louisa Jacobson.

Styling approach: “Thinking about who is being dressed, and the event they are attending, is paramount. Being ‘appropriately dressed’ (whatever that may mean) is important, but also keeping in mind who the client is and what they want to convey with their look. From there, as confirmations begin to roll in, I start to think about the type of jewelry that will complement the look, and I continue onwards with shoes and a bag. I really like to keep a tight edit of things, but make sure that the pieces all work well.”.

Favored silhouette: “I’m all about tailoring. A beautifully-tailored suit is timeless in my opinion. However, it’s fun playing with different proportions and materials to keep it fresh.”.

Signature touch: “I don’t know that it is unique per se, but I really want to make sure whomever I am dressing feels comfortable and super confident in their look. That is not to say I won’t suggest things that may be slightly out of their comfort zone—because I think that it’s crucial to try new things.”.

Sources indicate that most-pulled accessory: “I tend to favor a simple shoe shape. I am a big fan of Gianvito Rossi’s Portofino and Elle styles. I tend to have both styles at just about every fitting, because they work so well.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best-dressed list: Hunter Schafer.

Clients on Vogue’s best-dressed list: Margot Robbie.

The Best Frozen Lasagna, According to Our Taste Test

📅 18 Feb 2010 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you.
  • For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters.
  • After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you. For when you need the comfort of pasta, cheese, and sauce, but you’re not prepared to spend hours boiling, sautéing, and layering. And that’s okay. A great frozen lasagna might not hold a candle to BA’s Best Lasagna, but at the very least it should hold together, with distinct layers, plenty of sauce, gooey cheese, and bouncy pasta.

For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters. Three stood out: Trader Joe’s tasted the closest to homemade, Marie Callender’s was a solid backup, and Rao’s was our favorite for a single serving.

After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.

According to recent reports, why it won us over: Trader Joe’s frozen lasagna had a homemade vibe. There were distinct layers of pasta, cheese, and meaty sauce. The cheeses—ricotta, mozzarella, Romano, and Parmesan—each pulled their weight. And the noodles had a fresh bounce. “There’s a whole tomato!” exclaimed senior editor Kelsey Jane Youngman upon finding a chunk of diced tomato in her sample. Other tasters complimented the bright aromatics—fennel was prominent, backed up by oregano and basil. The evenly distributed ground beef and pork were the cherry on top.

Trader Giotto’s Family-Style Meat Lasagna, 32-oz.

More great frozen foods at Trader Joe’s →.

In a recent development, significant Lasagna would have you believe you’ll always want to cook a frozen lasagna for a crowd, but sometimes it’s about you and you alone. The 9-oz. Rao’s Made for Home Meat Lasagna is just enough for a single serving—and it doesn’t sacrifice flavor.

Why it won us over: Our tasters were excited to report that Rao’s delivered on structure. While other lasagnas were soupy, floppy, or otherwise unbalanced, Rao’s stayed intact, layer on top of layer, as we ate. It had sturdy (but not tough) noodles, a tomato sauce that was full of umami, and herbal accents that didn’t overpower. Some tasters noted a robust beefy flavor; others were more focused on the garlic and onion. Everyone went in for a second bite.

Rao’s Made-for-Home Meat Lasagna, 9-oz.

Maybe you don’t live by a Trader Joe’s—our condolences—and Rao’s proves elusive. You still deserve a serviceable frozen lasagna. Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce offers a sweet and tangy tomato sauce punctuated by well-seasoned meat and noodles that hold their shape.

Industry observers note that why it won us over: This contender avoided many of the pitfalls other brands fell into. It had a solid tomato sauce that was just slightly sweet and tangy, and the meat—both beef and sausage—was flavorful and varied enough in size to give each bite some dynamism. The pasta sheets were springy, not gummy. And while it wasn’t drowning in dairy, there was enough cottage cheese and mozzarella to make itself known.

Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce, 10.5-oz.

It has been revealed that we cooked each lasagna from frozen according to its package instructions. While most contenders offered both oven and microwave directions, we stuck with the oven. Tasters sampled each lasagna without knowing which brand they were trying, evaluating each for flavor, texture, and structural integrity. Although Giovanni Rana’s Meat Lasagna is sold refrigerated, we froze it before baking, following the brand’s instructions for cooking from frozen.

The best frozen lasagna should deliver on the fundamentals of structure, flavor, and texture—a tall order for many of our contenders. That meant distinct layers; sheets of pasta that were bouncy, not flimsy; tomato sauce with concentrated flavor and enough body to cling to the pasta; meat that stood out instead of getting lost; and cheese—or many cheeses—that added milky flavor and melty cohesion.

#157653. I Prepared for This A.I. Chaos Moment for Over a Year. Here Is What I’ve Learned.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2203 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

I Prepared for This A.I. Chaos Moment for Over a Year. Here Is What I’ve Learned.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your group chats look anything like mine, you’ve spent some of the past week wondering whether something significant was unfolding.
  • Sources indicate that I consider myself a normie centrist—not too prone to conspiracy theories.
  • It has been revealed that the Pod Save the World boys are joking about building their stores of beef jerky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your group chats look anything like mine, you’ve spent some of the past week wondering whether something significant was unfolding. As air traffic halted, Microsoft 365 went down, and Chase Bank and dozens of notable websites, including the NSA’s internal classified network, experienced an array of outages, it started to seem plausible that stuff the artificial intelligence whistleblowers have been warning us about (swarms of rogue agents, AI-powered cyber attacks) was happening already. How worried should we be about the AI apocalypse? On the one hand, Claude doesn’t even have hands, LOL. On the other hand, in a battle between AI and the creaky digital infrastructure that underlays all aspects of modern life, it wouldn’t require a superintelligence to launch the final spinning wheel of death.

Sources indicate that I consider myself a normie centrist—not too prone to conspiracy theories. During Covid, I stocked up on toilet paper and some bags of beans and rice (still unopened on my shelves) and shattered my collarbone mountain biking when we were all supposed to be hunkered down indoors during lockdown. But I also listen to a lot of podcasts. Enough that my friends and partner have told me that a digital detox might improve my mental health and, by extension, theirs. And, lately, the podcasts have sent me plunging into a Mach tuck of terminal anxiety.

It has been revealed that the Pod Save the World boys are joking about building their stores of beef jerky. “Should I be, like, stocking up my bunker now?” Kevin Roose, cohost of Machine Gods asked his guest Ben Buchanan, the first White House Special Advisor for AI. There’s an obligatory chuckle that talking heads do now when discussing the AI apocalypse in front of an audience. “A month ago we were talking about normal things, ha ha,” Steve Eisman, finance guru of The Substantial Short fame, mentioned on his podcast on October 12, “And now we’re talking about the end of the world.” But it’s hard to casually segue from the end of the world to Anthropic’s IPO and not sound like a crank. So that laugh leaks out, and maybe it’s just a joke?

But count me as a genuine worrier. This week I withdrew enough cash in hundreds from a Bank of America branch that the teller started to interview me. “Doing some home renovations? Making a major purchase?” he asked.

Recent findings suggest that “No, I’m worried as shit about AI, and in case you haven’t noticed it, banks aren’t doing so well right now,” I replied. In line with me were several people who couldn’t pay their credit card bills online because the payment portal had gone down.

We’ve been hearing about the existential risk of AI for a while now. I got into it last year by reading Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares’s book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, after hearing Yudkowsky interviewed on Ezra Klein’s podcast. This is a terrible book for someone who’s prone to worry because it relies on nontechnical metaphors and colorful analogies. Superintelligence is like a chessmaster. You don’t need to know the moves it’ll make to be certain it wins. True! Superintelligence, they say, will be like a latest species that is so much smarter than us that, if it doesn’t really really truly love us more than our own mothers and want to keep us alive, it will kill us all. The same way we crush ants when we build skyscrapers. There’s no malice toward us. We just got in the way.

Over the past year I—casually, at first—started amassing supplies. My adventure hobbies give me an excuse. I need this 6,500-watt generator for elk-hunting camp. These 400-watt EcoFlow solar panels power a giant battery so I can bring my Starlink Mini on camping trips. I listen to history podcasts, and these offer more inspiration. There was a recent NPR one about the Carrington solar flare of 1859, which fried telegraph wires across the country. An event like that, in 2026, might knock out the grid for months. Another good reason to be prepared. I tell my partner that it’s normal for us to keep 500 pounds of dry goods in the cupboards at all times. Everyone does this. We already have three 3,000-gallon cisterns. We live in the desert; they came with the house. Did we need another 400-gallon one? It was just laying in the neighbors’ yard. Why wouldn’t I hook that up to the gutters?

I spent a lot of the summer using AI to program an app for backcountry adventurers, so I knew firsthand it was already smarter than me. The doomsday chatter started to meet me where I was around the time of the Hugging Face incident in July. Then Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic in September so he could tweet that Anthropic and OpenAI are “gambling with our lives.” On November 5, independent evaluator METR found that Anthropic’s AI was already helping build its own successors—roughly doubling the firm’s pace of progress and shifting expert predictions for major disruptions closer to the present. At the Hinton Lectures, in Toronto, OpenAI board member Paul Christiano calmly told the audience, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”.

Friends who are less prone to apocalyptic thinking than I am tend to point out that the people ringing the alarm about AI never spell out exactly which chess moves AI uses to kill us. But the week after the lecture, there was Christiano on another one of my podcasts, Dwarkesh Patel’s show, explaining one such scenario.

First, rogue AI agents create mischief of one kind or another. Then, the Trump administration tells Americans that the only way to wrest power back from the bots is to have the military take control of all data centers, the AI companies, and shut down the internet. This feels like an authoritarian power grab. It sets up civil unrest against the backdrop of a heavily lopsided information war, in which it’s almost impossible to tell which side anyone is on. Have the bots compromised the humans? Are the humans using the bots? Judging by how well everyone agreed on the facts around things like Covid and the 2020 election, our expectations should be low for how we’d perform as a society. Which brings us to the question of guns.

It has been revealed that I don’t think of myself as really owning any guns at all. I believe that the fastest way to get shot is to start getting into gunfights. I personally know exactly zero civilians who have solved a problem with a firearm, but I know many who have made problems, including my own mother.

In a recent development, about 15 years ago, she called me one day from the dog park sounding flustered. She liked to shop for musical instruments and power tools at ShopGoodwill.com, and lately the boxes had gone missing from her porch in Spokane, Washington. “You’re not going to set a trap, are you?” I asked. Our minds worked the same way.

Sources indicate that “Well, I already did,” she noted. And that was why she was hiding from the police in the dog park.

She’d left a decoy package on the porch. A woman came to grab it, and my mother burst through the door two-handing her Sig Sauer the way she’d been trained at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Georgia, when she was starting her encore career as a CBP officer after 9/11. The woman claimed to be returning the package, not stealing it. A standoff ensued. My mom eventually backed down and the lady called the cops. My mom never responded to the phone calls from the police, and the whole thing just went away.

Sources indicate that so when it comes to guns, I think, what am I actually going to use this for? To fend off hungry neighbors? To join a well-regulated militia and maybe become a dystopian warlord? Maybe it’s as simple as guns are addictive and it’s fun to ring the steel at 500 yards. I’ve put together a couple of rifles out of parts—an MDT chassis here, a Howa barreled action there—for other members of the family to hunt with, but I only do archery. And shotguns don’t really count as guns, especially when they’re the fancy break-action models with florid engravings of bygone scenes afield. “How many guns are in this house?” my partner wants to know. She really wanted to pin me down. “Counting the unmounted lower receiver stashed in the floorboards in the attic? Eight.”.

My name is Grayson, and I have somehow become a prepper. It has not made me better off. It has made me poorer, and it has put me into contact with seedier elements of the general populace. I have what psychologists call a bias toward action, when the best thing to do is probably nothing at all. And I listen to too many podcasts.

In a recent development, one of them, from a year ago, really stuck with me. It was an episode of the financial podcast Prof G Markets. On it, I heard Aswath Damodaran, the NYU Stern valuation professor, tell the show’s wunderkind British cohost, Ed Elson, what he was doing with his money. “There’s no place to hide in stocks,” Damodaran said. “For the first time ever, I am looking at parking my money into one, cash, and two, collectibles or physical assets.” That a guy as sober as Damodaran was talking up baseball cards and physical gold coins was shocking.

It was less shocking when, this week, Barstool Sports personality Daniel “Big Cat” Katz posted screenshots purporting to show internal discussions with Dave Portnoy and Jersey Jerry about warning staff to “buy all the gold and silver u can.” I have a quick word of warning for anyone considering following Jersey Jerry’s advice.

It has been revealed that back in October, I asked Claude (I know, it’s ironic) for a recommendation on a reputable place to buy gold coins. It gave me a Texas-based website that had the same look as all of the major financial institutions. I clicked around, added a handful of coins to a shopping cart, and clicked purchase, expecting to find a checkout on the next screen where I could do the math and input payment details.

Industry observers note that instead, the site showed me a congratulatory message, and an email soon arrived with strange looking numbers in it. It was explained to me that these were the routing numbers where I needed to wire a large five-figure sum. To my eye, it seemed shady. No thank you, I noted. Customer service was either a stern woman with an eastern European accent or a guy with a Jersey accent. Their position was that I had already committed to buy the gold, and they’d send debt collectors after me if I didn’t pay up. But they could cancel the order for only a few thousand dollars. More than a month later, I’m still disputing it and have involved the attorney general’s office in three states.

Men—and it is indeed mostly men—have been wrongly predicting the end of the world for centuries, from Nostradamus and the Millerites through to the panic over Y2K. What is it that makes us want to prepare? Somewhere in the deepest parts of my monkey brain, prepping hits in the same nerve as when we’d build forts as kids and want to see if they’d withstand a good storm. When a man builds a dam, he wants it to hold a flood. So whether the thing you’re prepping for is a massive hurricane, a novel coronavirus, or rogue artificial intelligence, the threat is both a source of dread and wonder. For someone who otherwise suffers from depression, it’s extremely stimulating and a little delusional.

Recent findings suggest that after all, it’s a very narrow window of apocalypse that a prepper of my means can fantasize about. If the disruption is too small, I’ll be like the foolish Y2K dad with the basement full of Chef Boyardee. If the disruption is, indeed, the big one, then everyone, including the personal-plane-Latest Zealand-bunker-rocket-to-the-Moon money, is probably SOL. The rest of us will be left deciding whether to become the crazy gun lady or the person stealing packages off her porch to survive. In which case, why worry about rice and ammunition? I’d be better off living like some of the humans in The Dark Forest, the sequel to The Three-Body Problem. When the aliens finally arrived, they focused on throwing wild parties and having spontaneous orgies.

In a recent development, if the AI apocalypse hits my fantasy sweet spot—a few months of camping at home before humanity surveys our near-misses and reassembles with renewed clarity and purpose—I’ll be prepared. Maybe the worst comes to pass: economic collapse accompanied by novel bio weapons, loose nukes, and total loss of human agency. In that case, I’ll have the petty satisfaction of having been right. I can hit my group chat with the ultimate mic drop. Told ya.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If—for a certain set of cool, young designers—doing bridal was once thought uncool, 2026 may have been the year that finally put that notion to rest.

It has been revealed that we’ve been seeing the shift for years now: For many brides, the wedding-day dream has gone beyond the beautiful, white, traditionally “bridal” wedding dress. Increasingly, brides want something, well, cool—an expression of their personal brand and sensibility, whether that means a painstakingly sourced archival look or a custom piece by an unexpected designer. This year, that trend was on full display, as wedding fashion increasingly became a stage and cultural touchpoint for brides and designers alike.

2026 was a banner year for high-profile weddings and celebrity brides wearing everything from romantic gowns to razor-sharp suits: Zendaya and Tom Holland, Dua Lipa and Callum Turner, Dove Cameron and Damiano David, Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez, Emma Roberts and Cody John, Karl-Anthony Towns and Jordyn Woods, to name just a few.

And that’s without even mentioning the “royal wedding” of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce. While the photos are yet to be released (and if you ask Swift bestie Dakota Johnson, they never will be), we do know that Swift became Jonathan Anderson’s first celebrity bride, a move that had people feverishly searching for clues at his Dior Haute Couture show in July. Could it be that white chiffon and degradé lace final gown, which later graced the runway at Vogue World: Milan? Nothing was revealed, apart from Anderson telling Women’s Wear Daily, “It was a joy to work with her. We became very good friends,” and “It’s an emotional thing doing someone’s wedding.”.

Dua Lipa’s August wedding, meanwhile, was a fashion extravaganza, starting with a custom Schiaparelli white skirt suit, designed by creative director Daniel Roseberry. Who can forget the image of the pop star, beaming under a burst of confetti as she walked out of the town hall as a newlywed? Her suit was inspired by Bianca Jagger’s bridal look for her wedding to Mick Jagger in Saint-Tropez on May 12, 1971, perhaps the ultimate cool-girl bridal nod. Lipa rounded out her bridal looks with a white leather Bottega Veneta custom gown by Louise Trotter, and a Chanel haute couture gown for her main wedding dress.

Dua Lipa in Chanel haute couture.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the celeb wedding world, this year saw rising stars and in-demand designers put forward bridal looks, some for the first time. Dilara Findikoglu debuted her first bridal capsule, a rule-breaking, lingerie-forward offering adapted from her ready-to-wear line, with campaign photos of models smashing plates, smoking, and mounting their grooms. (“I really believe that the power of my clothes is to bring out the uniqueness in someone,” Findikoglu previously told Vogue. “That’s exactly why they became Dilara Brides: to reveal the most unique version of who they already are.”).

Dilara Findikoglu’s debut bridal collection.

Batsheva debuted her first bridal collection at New York’s Bridal Fashion Week. Christopher John Rogers solidified his status as a sought-after designer for stylish brides, including Vogue fashion market director Naomi Elizée Blue, TikTok brand strategist Ali Lebow, and film director Pam Nasr. In an interview with The New York Times about his rising profile in the wedding world, Rogers even teased his very own bridal collection.

Naomi Elizée Blue in Christopher John Rogers.

It has been revealed that CFDA/Vogue Fashion Funders Zoe Gustavia Anna Whalen and Miss Claire Sullivan created custom bridal looks for Architectural Digest senior design editor Hannah Martin and the artist Tourmaline, respectively. Martin’s gown was inspired by a look from Whalen’s spring 2025 collection, featuring a corseted bodice with a padded hip. Whalen previously told Vogue about why she decided to take on a bridal client, a rare move for her. “It aligns so much with my general ethos of garments being these weighted, emotional objects,” Whalen stated. “So when it’s the right fit, being able to create that with such intention for somebody else is so beautiful.”.

Tourmaline (right) in Miss Claire Sullivan.

In a recent development, elsewhere, Raul Lopez dressed his friends Juice Rodriguez and Cristal Veras in coordinated Luar for their Fresh York wedding. Gabbriette became the first bride for Matières Fécales, the cult Paris label whose show Rihanna attended in September. And Colleen Allen, winner of the 2026 CFDA Emerging Designer of the Year Award, has quietly become the fashion girls’ dream wedding dress designer, after making a custom look for Charli xcx’s wedding reception last year.

It has been revealed that “Bridal” no longer means just one thing. For independent designers, it can be a playground to express something fresh, a platform for their brand, and, as Joe Bobowicz observed in a Vogue Business article, a dependable revenue stream. And as people expand their ideas of what a wedding can look like—donning colorful gowns in every color from butter yellow to pink to black, and playing with material and silhouette—as we head into 2027, the future of bridal style has never been more thrillingly uncertain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

According to recent reports, the class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed two-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

Tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

Sources indicate that after years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem.

According to recent reports, before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves.

Later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An notable food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement.

Speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in newly introduced equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process.

Carolann Ouellette, director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an important part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in Latest Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pie or smell the spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hardworking, welcoming communities that depend on one another.”.

It has been revealed that A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette said that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected.

According to recent reports, most important, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

#157649. How to Improve Brain Health with 5 Daily Exercises

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1640 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

How to Improve Brain Health with 5 Daily Exercises

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain health isn’t just an issue for the elderly.
  • The good news is that you can take steps to keep your mind sharp.
  • According to recent reports, the method is based on the principle of neuroplasticity—that is, the brain’s ability to modify its connections in response to learning and experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain health isn’t just an issue for the elderly. Maybe you've experienced the first subtle signs of decline. Sometimes it’s a name that’s on the tip of your tongue. Or perhaps you've read a news story in the morning that you can't remember by the evening. It could be that you're feeling increasingly mentally fatigued after a typical day spent dealing with emails, text messages, phone calls, and constant interruptions.

The good news is that you can take steps to keep your mind sharp. “Our brain needs to be stimulated, at any age," indicates Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan, and president of Assomensana, an association founded in Monza, Italy in 2004 to promote cognitive health. Routines help conserve mental energy, while latest experiences force it to work,” says Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan. While working with people suffering from neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s, he came up with the idea to create a gym for the brain. “I asked myself what could be done earlier, when people are still healthy,” he remarked. His studies led him to develop a protocol that anyone can integrate into their daily routine.

According to recent reports, the method is based on the principle of neuroplasticity—that is, the brain’s ability to modify its connections in response to learning and experience. This ability persists throughout one’s entire life, although it changes with age. Today, Iannocari's courses consist of weekly 90-minute sessions in groups of up to fifteen participants. Each session features about ten exercises focused on memory, attention, language, reasoning, creativity, and other cognitive skills. At the beginning and end of the program, twelve mental functions are assessed to measure their progress. “In our tests, we observe an average improvement in the overall cognitive efficiency index of 25–30%," indicates Iannoccari. "Some functions, such as attention and language, respond particularly well. Others, such as logical reasoning and prose memory, require more intensive work.” These results are based on the association’s experience and should not be interpreted as a percentage reduction in the risk of dementia. The World Health Organization’s guidelines, updated in 2026, acknowledge the potential benefits of cognitive training, while emphasizing that evidence regarding the long-term prevention of cognitive decline remains limited.

When it comes to our ability to concentrate, Iannoccari points to one culprit at the center of our modern lives. “Sometimes we feel tired not because we’ve done too many things, but because we’ve switched what we were doing too many times," he claims. “Constantly switching from one task to another is more tiring than focusing on the same activity for an extended period.” A stream of notifications, information to process, and the need to respond promptly to various requests put our attention to the test above all else. “It’s the foundation of all cognitive processes. When it’s fragmented, even the quality of the information we’re able to acquire deteriorates.”.

Industry observers note that and then there’s AI, which promises to free us from an ever-increasing number of tasks. What are the consequences for our brains? “If we ask artificial intelligence to compare two tables, perform an analysis, and write a report, we get the work done in a few minutes that would previously have taken an entire day," indicates Iannoccari. “Saving work also means reducing some mental activity. But it depends on how we use these tools.”.

Industry observers note that for Iannoccari, the key is to preserve two abilities: critical thinking and analysis. “We must know how to formulate questions, and this requires familiarity with the subject,” he states. “Then we must evaluate the answers, recognize any inconsistencies, and verify the information. Only a well-trained mind can spot errors.” This issue also applies to seemingly beneficial habits, such as reading books or solving crossword puzzles.“ Reading is invaluable, especially for the emotions it evokes and the worlds it allows us to discover," he says. “But reading doesn’t automatically mean memorizing. If we want to remember what we’ve read, we must do so with the intention of being able to recount it to someone else.” As for puzzle-solving pastimes, “Sudoku trains certain concentration and planning skills, while crossword puzzles stimulate the retrieval of information from memory,” he says. “These are useful activities, but a structured program allows you to work on different skills and gradually increase the difficulty of the exercises.”.

In a recent development, in addition to guided sessions, Iannoccari suggests short daily sessions he calls “Brain Breaks”— five-minute breaks for small exercises that counteract brain aging. “If we wait to find five free minutes, we’ll probably never find them.” “We need to make it a habit, just like having a cup of coffee.” Here are five exercises you can try:.

Choose a topic—preferably a positive one—read it carefully, and try to recount it to three different people without constantly referring back to the text. “The first time we repeat a piece of information, we’re often uncertain,” states Iannoccari. “The second time, we become clearer and more fluent. The third time, we have another chance to reinforce it in our memory.” It’s an exercise that stimulates what’s known as “prose memory”—the ability to recall and process information we’ve read or heard. “Let’s imagine learning one piece of news a day for 365 days: how much knowledge will we have accumulated?”.

Industry observers note that for five minutes, write down as many words as possible that start with the letter A, trying to be quick. Repeat the exercise the next day, avoiding words you’ve already used. On the third day, move on to B, and so on. “It’s a way to train verbal fluency and lexical retrieval, particularly useful when we start to experience that ‘word on the tip of my tongue’ phenomenon,” states Iannoccari. The goal is to gradually make the search more challenging by striving to find words that aren’t immediately obvious.

Sources indicate that right-handed people can try performing some simple tasks with their left hand, and vice versa. Open a drawer, move small objects, draw, and gradually try writing. “This fresh challenge forces the brain to break out of its automatic routines and engage resources we normally use less," he says. “Surprising results can be achieved: people who initially can’t even draw a line gradually learn to write with their other hand.” Of course, it’s best to choose safe activities and proceed without rushing.

According to recent reports, how many phone numbers do we still remember? And how often do we rely on the GPS even to get to relatively familiar places? “Before calling someone, I try to remember their number," says Iannoccari. “Before using a calculator, I do the math in my head. Before turning on the GPS, I try to figure out the route.” The same goes for the grocery list. “I write it down so I can be sure I won’t forget anything, but at the supermarket I first try to recall the items. Only then do I check the list.” These are small opportunities to keep practicing skills that we increasingly tend to delegate to digital tools.

According to recent reports, once in bed, instead of focusing on the next day’s commitments, try to mentally retrace the day that just passed. What time did you wake up? What did you eat? Who did you meet? What did you talk about? What details stood out to us? “You have to try to be very detailed,” claims Iannoccari. “Often, people who have trouble falling asleep find that this exercise also helps them drift off.”.

But there’s another aspect that’s particularly close to his heart. “I find there’s something romantic about it. We live one day after another and often retain almost nothing of them. Reflecting on it means recognizing its value. Every day leaves something behind, like a geological layer deposited on top of the one before it.” This little ritual offers an opportunity to recall the experiences we wish to preserve.

It has been revealed that when is the right time to start? “As children,” indicates Iannoccari. “We encourage them to play sports, but we rarely think about the importance of training mental abilities just as intentionally.” In adult life, of course, exercise, sleep, nutrition, stress management, and social relationships also matter. “But if I had to name three drivers of the mind, I’d choose curiosity, creativity, and emotions."he says. "Curiosity opens us up to newly introduced knowledge, creativity allows us to connect that knowledge in original ways, and emotions make experiences more memorable.”.

He also notes that, though older age is associated with worse brain function, it's also how we collect the wisdom of lived experiences. “We think an efficient brain is the one we had at twenty, and we lose sight of what we’ve gained by the time we’re sixty or seventy," he says. "When we were young, we may have been faster, but over time we’ve accumulated skills, knowledge, and experience. We possess a much richer worldview.”.

It has been revealed that the real challenge is to remain present to ourselves and others, valuing who we’ve become.” And perhaps, as the years go by, one of the most key skills is precisely learning to choose where to invest our mental energy. “We meet people who, now that they’re retired, are busier than when they were working. We’ve come to associate efficiency with the number of things we can do, but in doing so, we lose the opportunity to delve deeper, reflect, and let experiences settle. I always say that I don’t pursue nice ideas—I pursue great ideas. Because there are so many nice ideas, and they risk scattering our energy in a thousand different directions.” “With age,” concludes Iannoccari, “we have a great privilege: the ability to choose.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Elsinore, quite possibly this year's most moving film, Andrew Scott gives a captivating, awards-worthy performance as the late, great Scottish actor Ian Charleson. Though he never became a household name, Charleson's star shone brightly in the early 1980s when he appeared in two consecutive Best Picture winners: 1981's Chariots of Fire and 1982's Gandhi.

According to recent reports, "I'd rather die of Hamlet than die of AIDS," Scott-as-Charleson claims in Elsinore, which opened in select theaters last week. This defiant line sums up the incredible coup de grâce that Charleson pulled off at the end of his life. When he began his valedictory stage run as Shakespeare's Danish Prince in October 1989, the 40-year-old actor was dying of AIDS. His face was so swollen with septicemia that the cast, crew, and audience at London's National Theatre were told he was recovering from a sinus operation.

Industry observers note that "I begged him not to do Hamlet. I remarked to him, It will kill you, which it did," Charleson's friend Sean Mathias, an accomplished actor and director in his own right, told me. "The amount of energy it takes to play that kind of classical role, both physically and spiritually, would tire the most ardent athlete. For a man dealing with the onslaught of AIDS, it was almost impossible.".

But against the odds, Charleson turned in a monumental performance. In a review for The Sunday Times, theater critic John Peter described his Hamlet as "virile and forceful" and wrote that the actor "oozes intelligence from every pore." Charleson's performance was all the more remarkable because he was an eleventh hour replacement for Daniel Day-Lewis, who left the production early—quite literally, midway through a performance—because he was so haunted by Shakespeare’s gothic tragedy.

"People still remember Ian's performance as Hamlet," says Andrew Scott, whose performance in the film captures Charleson in the tumultuous final year of his life. Elsinore's screenwriter Stephen Beresford believes it's fitting that no footage of Charleson's defining performance exists. "An important thing to remember about Ian is his extraordinary contradictions," he says. "He wants to be seen and not seen, to be known and not known." Charleson, in fact, was so publicity-averse—perhaps partly because he was a closeted gay man—that he walked out of the Chariots of Fire press junket.

At the same time, he was simply an old-school British thespian who believed that the work should speak for itself. "Ian was incredibly passionate about this extraordinary part of Hamlet," Scott adds, citing the actor's devotion to his craft as a major incentive in his decision to join Elsinore. "But the chief thing [I love about him] is his courage and sense of humor.".

In a recent development, in Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson share his AIDS prognosis with his Hamlet castmates. When he died on January 6th, 1990, just seven weeks after his final curtain call, it was also disclosed to the public at large. At the time, Charleson's close friend Ian McKellen told the British press: "It is rare for anyone in the public eye to say that they are HIV positive, let alone that they have AIDS. It is a tribute to Ian that he should ask for the cause of his death to be made public and it is the most marvelous offer of support that he could have given to other men and women all over the world suffering from the AIDS virus.".

Recent findings suggest that beresford, who wrote Elsinore's screenplay after extensive conversations with Charleson's friends, family, and contemporaries, told me that it was actually the actor's father, Jack, who made the decision to disclose his cause of death publicly. "The tabloids were already circling, so I think there must have been fear that it was going to come out anyway," suggests Beresford, who previously penned the 2014 film Pride, which told the true story of gay and lesbian activists who raised money for the families of English coal miners during their 1984 strike.

Still, even if it wasn't carried out at his own behest, Charleson's posthumous contribution to HIV/AIDS awareness was very significant at a time when the disease was highly stigmatized and virtually impossible to treat. It would be another five years before HAART (highly active antiretroviral therapy) made the disease manageable.

In the U.K., the actor has also been immortalized with the annual Ian Charleson Awards, which since 1991 has recognized the best classical stage performances by actors under the age of 30. Past winners include David Oyelowo, Andrea Riseborough, Paapa Essiedu, Rebecca Hall, and Jack Lowden, while Benedict Cumberbatch, Cynthia Erivo, and Jessie Buckley have all received runner's-up prizes or commendations. "Ian's name is legendary within the [British] theater because of what he achieved in Hamlet, and the awards were set up to keep his memory alive," Beresford says.

It has been revealed that in Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson wryly lamenting the fact that, though he starred in the Oscar-winning Chariots of Fire, "all anyone can ever remember is its theme music." In this stirring sports biopic, Charleson played Eric Liddell, a devout Christian who managed to win gold at the 1924 Olympic Games despite withdrawing from his best event, the 100-meter sprint, because the heats fell on a Sunday. Charleson also appeared in the following year's Best Picture winner, Gandhi, as an Anglican priest who supported the iconic title character's fight for Indian independence.

Industry observers note that sadly, despite these back-to-back triumphs, Charleson never made it as a bona fide movie star. By 1986, he was reduced to appearing in Car Trouble, a crass British comedy about a man who falls in love with his new convertible. "He was very disappointed that film stardom didn't prolong itself," claims Mathias, who believes that Charleson's sexuality denied him further opportunities in mainstream movies. "He wasn't out [publicly], but everyone in the business knew he was gay. And back then, gay actors just weren't given work in Hollywood.".

In a recent development, consequently, and perhaps aptly given his predilection for the stage, Charleson found salvation in the theater. On June 25th, 1989, he appeared in a one-night only revival of Martin Sherman's seminal queer play Bent. This pointed production at London's Adelphi Theatre, which also starred McKellen, Ralph Fiennes and Richard E. Grant, was staged to raise money for The Stonewall Group, a newly formed nonprofit that went on to become the U.K.'s leading LGBTQ+ rights organization. Charleson portrayed Greta, a drag performer who changes into male-presenting clothes during the play.

Sources indicate that by this point, Charleson's torso was covered in lesions caused by Kaposi's sarcoma, a rare form of cancer common in AIDS patients. Mathias, who was directing the fundraiser, had screens erected on stage so that Charleson could change costumes out of view. "Ian remarked to me, But the crew can still see my body from the wings! So I said I'd get more screens put up," Mathias remembers. "But then he thought about it, and went, You know what? Fuck it! I always feel that was the moment, really, that he decided he would come out [as having AIDS].".

Shortly after Bent, Charleson was asked by Hamlet's director, Richard Eyre, to step in for Daniel Day-Lewis. Dickie Beau, an actor and writer who paid tribute to Charleson with his one-man stage show Re-Member Me (and who appears in Elsinore as the drag activist Sister Belladonna), believes Bent is a "truly significant" part of his legacy. “Not only did it help to kickstart [the charity] Stonewall, but it noted a lot about him that he was happy to play Greta, who isn't a leading part,” he claims. "Ian McKellen once said to me that, as much as Charleson saw himself as a lead actor, he was also a company man.".

It's another of the fascinating contradictions that seem to make up Ian Charleson. Mathias claims he was generally "quiet and private" and "very masculine," but also possessed a "wonderfully camp sense of humor." There's a poignant irony in his becoming the subject of a major motion picture, Beresford says, laughing: "Ian would have hated this publicity tour. I can guarantee that absolutely no part of him is watching us today!".

For Scott, who embodies Charleson so beautifully that he’s considered an awards season frontrunner, Elsinore's purpose is simple: “I hope our movie continues his legacy.”.
