Sources indicate that divinity candy is a classic Southern dessert. If you haven't heard of it yet, I promise you'll be coming back to this recipe over and over again after making it just once! It’s a simple confection made of sugar, eggs, and corn syrup that looks like clouds, with the crunch of meringue and the chew of a perfect marshmallow. It does require a candy thermometer and a bit of patience, but once you know what to look for, it’s extremely simple to make.

In the large bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment, combine the egg whites and salt.

It has been revealed that in a medium pot, combine the sugar, corn syrup, and water. Attach a candy thermometer to the pot before you go any further. Heat the mixture over medium-high heat, undisturbed, until the thermometer registers 250°, which should take about 10 minutes. When the thermometer registers 235°, start whipping egg whites on high speed until stiff peaks form, which should take another 2 to 3 minutes.

With the mixer running on medium speed, carefully add sugar syrup to egg whites in a thin stream. Make sure to go slowly! The whole process should take about 1 to 2 minutes. Then beat in the vanilla extract.

Industry observers note that proceed to increase mixer speed to high and continue to whip until the mixture comes together and loses some of its gloss, which should take approximately 5 to 10 minutes. Let it all cool until the mixture is slightly thickened and holds its form when spooned onto parchment, another 1 to 2 minutes.

Grease 2 spoons with cooking spray, and working rapidly, spoon candy onto a parchment-lined baking sheet. Swirl it as desired to make the shapes you want! Immediately top the dessert with sprinkles. (The sprinkles won’t stick if you wait too long!).

It has been revealed that let the candy sit until it’s completely dry, just about 2 hours more. Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1 week and enjoy!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!).

More high-protein breakfast recipes here.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

Cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

According to recent reports, pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

According to recent reports, just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

Brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to Best Dressed, it's not all about the threads, the baubles deserve their due, too. Scanning Vogue's illustrious 2026 list, we noticed that several of our honorees have a particular penchant for accessorizing, and an equally impressive command of the historical reference. Take Margot Robbie, who borrowed Elizabeth Taylor's Taj Mahal diamond for the Los Angeles premiere of Wuthering Heights, while Céline Dion revisited her own fashion history during her Paris residency, commissioning a upcoming version of the Chanel Comète necklace she wore to the 1997 Oscars.

And the stories don't end there. From Colman Domingo's exuberant brooches to Zoë Kravitz's decidedly nonchalant approach to wearing enormous diamonds, this year's Best Dressed honorees know that jewelry can be as revealing of personal style as the clothes themselves. Whether it's a sentimental keepsake, a historical curiosity, or a spectacular feat of craftsmanship, these are the jewels that deserve a closer look.

For the Los Angeles premiere of Wuthering Heights in January, Margot Robbie paired her custom Schiaparelli gown with a piece of Hollywood history: Elizabeth Taylor's Taj Mahal diamond. The heart-shaped stone, suspended from a Cartier necklace, was a gift from Richard Burton to Taylor for her 40th birthday in 1972. With its associations of grand romance and one of Hollywood's most famously tempestuous love affairs, it was an inspired choice for a film about Catherine and Heathcliff. And Robbie's jewelry references didn't end there. At the London premiere, she wore a reproduction of Charlotte Brontë's mourning bracelet, whose original contained hair believed to belong to her sisters Emily and Anne. Clearly, someone had done their literary homework.

Céline Dion has never been one to shy away from a spectacular jewel, but her choices during her triumphant return to the stage in Paris came with more than a little sentiment. For her opening performance, she wore Boucheron's The Address necklace, a black-lacquer-and-diamond creation featuring a 10.01-carat emerald-cut diamond. The connection was deeply personal: her late husband, René Angélil, always wore Boucheron fragrance, and Dion noted the necklace made her feel as though he were with her.

Sources indicate that then, in October, Dion revisited a defining moment in her own fashion history. In 1997, she became the first artist to perform twice at a single Oscars ceremony, doing so in a plunging silver Chanel gown by Karl Lagerfeld and a celestial Comète necklace. Nearly three decades later, Matthieu Blazy reimagined the gown for her Paris residency, complete with a latest version of the necklace. Inspired by Gabrielle Chanel's original 1932 high-jewelry design, the piece featured 1,080 diamonds totaling more than 67 carats, set in platinum and white gold. Some things really are worth repeating.

It has been revealed that zendaya and longtime stylist Law Roach have made something of a specialty of dressing for the part, and their jewelry choices are no exception. There was the Bulgari Serpenti necklace, complete with a 93.83-carat emerald, at the 2021 Venice premiere of Dune, and the spectacular Chopard diamond bib worn with a sculptural Schiaparelli breastplate for The Odyssey this year. (Let’s not forget those controversial ancient Iranian gold medallion earrings that got people talking.) But perhaps her most intriguing accessory appeared during the Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day press tour in Shanghai: a diamond-set spider brooch with a yellow sapphire at its center, pinned to an archival Atelier Versace gown. The reference was obvious enough, but the provenance proved rather more complicated when two jewelry houses claimed credit for the jewel. The brooch was eventually traced to David Webb, though precisely how it ended up on Zendaya’s hip remains a mystery. A tangled web, indeed!

Industry observers note that few men have done more for the brooch in recent years than Colman Domingo. At the 2026 Emmys, he pinned Boucheron's Green Garden brooch, an extravagant arrangement of green tourmalines, diamonds, and green lacquer, to the fuchsia sash of his custom Valentino ensemble by Alessandro Michele. The piece comes from Boucheron's Like a Queen collection, inspired by a double-clip brooch given to Princess Elizabeth for her 18th birthday. Domingo's appreciation for jewelry history runs deep: at the 2025 Oscars, he wore a Boucheron ribbon brooch dating to 1956, while his 2025 Met Gala look featured the house's dramatic rock-crystal-and-diamond Iceberg necklace. Evidently, he sees no reason to leave the family jewels to the ladies.

Industry observers note that zoë Kravitz has a particular talent for making extraordinary jewelry look like something she just threw on. Case in point: the 20-carat Jessica McCormack diamond pendant she wore on a simple black cord for an appearance on Late Night with Seth Meyers last summer, paired with a cropped Saint Laurent vest, low-slung pinstripe trousers, and a bandana. As the jeweler's first-ever ambassador, Kravitz has made a convincing case for wearing serious diamonds with decidedly casual ease. At the 2026 Met Gala, she took a more surrealist approach, pairing her black lace Saint Laurent gown with McCormack's bespoke Medallion Cry Baby earrings and matching ring. Inspired by the imagery of Man Ray and Salvador Dalí, the earrings featured diamond tears suspended from golden eyes.

Industry observers note that leave it to Cole Escola to turn a piece of antique jewelry into a theatrical history lesson. At the 2025 Tony Awards, the Oh, Mary! playwright and star wore a custom ice-blue Wiederhoeft gown inspired by the costume Bernadette Peters wore to accept her Tony for Annie Get Your Gun in 1999. But the real deep cut was around Escola's neck: an antique pendant containing a portrait of Laura Keene, the actress and theater manager who was starring in Our American Cousin at Ford's Theatre on the night Abraham Lincoln was assassinated. The reference was particularly apt for the creator of a comedy about Mary Todd Lincoln, and hardly a casual choice. Escola has even spoken of visiting Keene's grave since Oh, Mary! opened.

In a recent development, chase Sui Wonders has developed a fondness for Tiffany & Co.'s feathered friends. At the 2026 Venice Film Festival, she wore Jean Schlumberger's iconic Bird on a Rock brooch, featuring a diamond of more than 13 carats and a pink sapphire, pinned to a simple ribbon around her neck. It was an inventive way to wear a design that dates back to 1965, and considerably more interesting than an ordinary diamond necklace. At the Actor Awards earlier in the year, she had opted for another interpretation of the house's avian motif: a Bird on a Rock necklace set with a 12-carat rubellite, accompanied by diamond-and-rubellite earrings totaling more than 33 carats.

What The Altruists Gets Right About Tech Scammers Like Sam Bankman-Fried

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the math holding up Netflix’s The Altruists is simple.
  • Famously, no bankers were sent to prison in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis.
  • It has been revealed that one of the threads in the journalism about the crimes, and on The Altruists, is that our power couple did not feel good in fancy spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the math holding up Netflix’s The Altruists is simple. Anthony Boyle plays at the moment imprisoned one-time cryptocurrency king Sam Bankman-Fried, and Julia Garner plays Caroline Ellison, fellow momentary crypto royal and Bankman-Fried’s one-time romantic partner. Both actors cook so fearlessly that the show’s shortcomings recede into the background. What you’re left with is a tidy sum: two excellent performances that offer rich, vatic examinations of real-life figures. From these visions of Bankman-Fried and Ellison we get a glimpse into a crime and into a psychology.

Famously, no bankers were sent to prison in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. No suit from Countrywide Financial walked the yard in Lompoc. But Samuel Bankman-Fried did go to prison after being found guilty of wire fraud and conspiracy. For the Bloomberg set, his trial was covered as intensely as O.J. Simpson’s, and each day of it hit trip wires: polycules, blockchain, non-fiat currency, etc.

It has been revealed that one of the threads in the journalism about the crimes, and on The Altruists, is that our power couple did not feel good in fancy spaces. But unlike the protagonists of so many other shows and movies from the tech-disruptor-story boom of the past 15 years, neither Boyle’s SBF nor Garner’s Ellison lean into rage.

On The Altruists, SBF and his inner circle frequent a Margaritaville in the Bahamas. They seem happy there, or at least at home. To be wildly rich, extremely young, and crushing vegan nachos at Jimmy Buffett’s theme restaurant is a choice made out of avoidance.

The show’s first episodes make clear the overlaps between Ellison and Bankman-Fried. They were true math minds surrounded by the glib Wharton crowd, goofs with board games. They were not-conventionally-attractive people in an industry where many people are quite hot, and where the primarily hot at least know which regression tool best fits what task.

It has been revealed that the Altruists’s versions of SBF and Ellison found love in a hopeless place. Boyle interviews Garner for a position at Jane Street and they realize they have the exact same investment strategy—all in, all the time. If you didn’t know better, you’d be rooting for these two off-putting lovebirds to make a go of it.

In a recent development, boyle’s performance mesmerizes. He seems to have control over his lashes, so completely articulated is his eye acting. His whole posture changes as he takes up different roles in the story: a curious loser, a gifted rhetorician, an anxious boss, an ignored former lover. The show shifts from alienation in Latest York to crypto adventures in Hong Kong to the office-dorm hybrid of “The Orchid” in the Bahamas. Boyle owns the physical transformations, letting the glee of the Hong Kong era fester into the eyebags and stress-weight accrued (probably one of the more ethical uses of a bodysuit I can recall) in the scheme’s last days.

Garner, meanwhile, has entered rarified air as a TV actor. Over the course of her career she has given us a moody, adrift Gen X student (Kimmy on The Americans), a Millennial lady of rage trapped in her dumpy hometown (Ozark), and now two glimpses of the self-satisfied Zillenial scammer (Anna Delvey in Inventing Anna and The Altruists). Garner’s signature move as a performer is to fail to sublimate anger or distress. Her characters have their own idiosyncratic patterns of twitches and attempts at steely gazes. The brittle darkness inside each of them sings. Her TV career belongs next to those of Elisabeth Moss and America Ferrera and Walton Goggins. It is time that this was generally acknowledged.

According to recent reports, the supporting cast is solid, with one particular highlight. In the middle of The Altruist’s eight-episode run, we get an entire episode focused on Sam Trabucco, a college bestie of SBF, a former Alameda Research co-CEO, and an early cooperator with federal prosecutors once the wheels started falling off.

Recent findings suggest that alex Lawther plays Trabucco and almost walks off with the show. Lawther’s slight frame and self-searching candor give each line of dialogue intimacy. I first saw Lawther on Andor, playing Nemik, idealistic proto-Rebel and truest of true believers, a character based on Lei Feng, the Chinese communist folk hero and soldier, who, like Nemik on Andor, died in a freak accident but left behind a diary of such pure faith that it became a recruitment tool for the revolution. (A recording of Lawther reading that manifesto from his diary—his voice reedy and prophetic—literally haunts Imperial high command at the end of Andor.).

In a recent development, in maybe my favorite scene of The Altruists, Trabucco and Ellison get dinner together. They talk and realize their childhood paths intersected and diverged across metro Boston—the same math competitions, the same tests. But their hometowns were quite different. She was from Newton. He was from Natick. If you’re from New England, that’s the only detail you need. (If you aren’t, I recommend Love Story and/or the novels of Dennis Lehane for background.) At that dinner, Lawther shares a deep, specific childhood memory of his father and Garner’s Caroline flinches without breaking eye contact, like she’s watching a recording of a natural disaster.

Industry observers note that sadly, the Netflix sins are here in full effect. The lighting is smeary and wildly off in many scenes. The music and sound mix could hardly be blunter. Even Oscar-nominated showrunner Graham Moore and talented directors like James Ponsoldt can’t lift dialogue that not-infrequently feels tailored to second-screen viewers: “They’re both off-the-charts math geniuses!”.

The braided narrative can turn single episodes into distracting puzzle boxes. The form is designed to function the way a major juicy 10,000-word legacy-media reported feature does: You know the ending, so it takes a memorable reshuffling of moments and incidents to create something newly introduced.

According to recent reports, but watching this gang of true believers and opportunists and criminally naïve teenage dream brains go from geographic zone to zone does carry emotional import. To them, and to The Altruists, the Bay Area has become a dated country club, a mirror image of The Social Network’s version of Harvard from the 2000s, back when the Bay Area promised something fresh. Post-Recession New York is greyscale normie central. Hong Kong and Macau blur together. The show ends in the Bahamas, a place that rich outsiders have always treated as both Eden and the afterlife.

Recent findings suggest that I think the era of the tech-bro-scammer-titan show and movie is reaching its end. If its dawn was The Social Network, the unrepeatable, mesmerizing You Can See Everything might be the sunset. Gen X icons Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher once tried to get their heads around millennial narcissism and now millennial genius Nathan Fielder has transformed his time with a real-deal apex-predator narcissist into a Möbius strip of content.

The drama of The Altruists depends on the psychology of the people who believe in crypto as a kind of syncretic faith. The show avoids a technical delineation of crypto itself, which makes sense. (I’ve yet to encounter a crypto evangelist who can provide a transparent explanation of the asset class that is superior to this.) ExxonMobil sells you a product and it works. Glock sells you a product and it works. Crypto works in so much as its existence justifies its existence. There are no earnings reports. Value is vibes.

Industry observers note that whenever something is being marketed as the future, it’s usually just the past, accelerated. People made crypto into an alternative financial system because they were “outsiders” who wanted to “disrupt.” Now the crypto system wants to be held close to the bosom of the enduring US financial markets and bulge bracket banks. A bill that would have brought them closer, setting up a regulatory framework, nose-dived in the senate.

According to recent reports, it sounds almost cowardly, like running home to mom and dad: We made a brave new thing better and cooler and freer than your corrupt old monetary system. A few years later: Let us back in and give us all the benefits of the old system! Get us in your PNC digital wallet, normie!

Bankman-Fried and Ellison are both the children of elite academics. To its credit, The Altruists pokes these Freudian pains. Bankman-Fried was raised by Stanford Law professors and chose MIT. Ellison was the child of MIT academics and chose Stanford. There’s self-belief in those exact choices. The children of faculty get a significant leg up in gaining admission at their parents’ institution. SBF and Ellison wanted to do something honest on their own, at least once.

Sources indicate that my parents are retired professors. You learn early on that you cannot possibly replicate your parents’ careers. A child of a lawyer can have their parent’s career 2.0. Same if you have doctors for parents. But truly successful academics—and given the market today, you either are truly successful or you don’t exist—create niches built only for one.

Sources indicate that successful academics eschew any number of linear career paths and lucrative fields to burrow into zones of learning where they have to be singular, own every network and endure any marginal post (Oregon State, thou hast thy music, too). To make it to a top institution, you need luck and power and timing to dovetail your own research record and professional charisma. Many people make it to powerful banks and hospitals and law firms. But if you manage to get tenure at Berkeley, you might really be that special.

The track record of the children of academics I know is messy: deluded guys floating around Portland or Boston trying to jam their unreadable YA series into the world, an acquaintance who self-sabotaged a promising, morally-clear career as a social worker because they did not get a doctorate and let that arbitrary marker of value smother their self-worth for decades.

SBF and Ellison were expected to perform precocity at all times, but the minute that they stumbled, Dr. Mom or Professor Dad stepped in with the better therapists and better lawyers to set everything right. The last two episodes of The Altruists bubble over with dread. Paul Reiser and Robin Weigert play SBF’s parents, and Jennifer Grey plays Caroline Ellison’s mom. Each performance puts its own spin on enmeshment and infantilization. The parents are not the big bads here. But they are the judgmental elitists who analyzed when they should have listened, and who raised these world-class scammers.

In a recent development, there was a guy a little like me in high school. Like me, he was the child of academics and teachers. Like me, he was clever and capable, which might have been enough in another high school. But such minor skills were door prizes in our grand, old, dizzyingly competitive boarding school. We both loved De La Soul. We were both cut from the same teams. We were both contrarians who trafficked in equal measures of insight and anserine bullshit. I won’t pretend to have been good friends with the guy—it was the classic situation where young men who play similar roles in their respective circles repel each other like the same sides of different magnets. But I sympathized. It’s painful to know exactly why you are not near the top of an elite ecosystem and then having to go on living in it.

I imagined he might have a career adjacent to mine. I imagined that we might see each other in the late 2000s at a Babygrande Records release party or in the bathroom at Santos Party House. It did not play out that way. A few years ago, during the inevitable age-related transition from Facebook to LinkedIn, the guy’s face and name swum across my screen. He’s become a significant deal in the crypto space. At one point, he rapped about crypto on crypto podcasts. On a class-wide group chat, as former classmates who had chosen to work in community health settings or on federally-funded research projects shared their pain after losing their jobs in the DOGE cuts, and as they voiced their concerns about what other digits of the American experiment would be severed next, this crypto dude commandeered the chat to brag about taking his firm public. No child of an academic has ever missed a chance to make it about them.

Recent findings suggest that one of the side effects of the world-gobbling narratives around A.I. (which gets its own Social Network moment in Luca Guadagnino’s imminent Artificial, with Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman) is that crypto already feels cringe—at best, a chrome decoration on the world-shaking machinery of LLMs and Deep Learning. The brave newly introduced world of private money that needed no society and no army behind it has become just another widget. The most vulgar people in the world trade meme coins with Turkish billionaire failsons. That Uber driver for whom you had great sympathy waits forever for a crypto ship that will never come into port. (Bankman-Fried, as it happens, was an early investor in Anthropic; it was reported last week that his shares, liquidated during FTX's bankruptcy, would be worth $35 to $37 billion in the wake of the AI lab's splashy IPO.).

If 2026 is the close of the tech-movie and tech-show era, then how do we square The Altruists? It has arrived at the end of something. It’s not perfect, maybe not even excellent, but it is effective and memorable, and provides a showcase for superb young actors. I wonder how many of these highlights about tech founders, disruptors, optimists, hustlers and misanthropes will last. The paranoia of 70s American film evaporated in the desert of 80s escapism and the wry smirk of Ronnie Reagan. The thorny, violent prestige TV era begat the soft-clothes forever-childhood of Stranger Things and of Ted Lasso. Legacy cannot be legislated in advance. I hope viewers check out The Altruists, and appreciate its gumption in allowing love—the least efficient of emotions—to animate the story.

According to recent reports, but maybe I’m wrong. Maybe I’ve been hustled by Boyle and Garner’s wonderful acting. Maybe my almost-instinct about the past 15 years of watching damaged young ladder-climbers and their digital dreams on screen is almost true: what will survive of us is coins.
